title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: The Sources of the General or Public Revenue of Society

A government has to cover the cost of defending the society and of maintaining the dignity of the chief magistrate, along with every other necessary expense of governing for which the state's constitution has set aside no particular revenue. That money can come from one of two places. The first is some fund that belongs specifically to the sovereign or the commonwealth and is independent of the people's own income. The second is the income of the people themselves.
Part I: The Funds, or Sources, of Revenue That May Belong Specifically to the Sovereign or Commonwealth
Any fund or source of revenue that belongs specifically to the sovereign or the commonwealth has to take one of two forms: capital stock or land.

A sovereign, like any other owner of capital, can draw a revenue from it in one of two ways: by putting it to work himself, or by lending it out. In the first case his revenue is profit; in the second it is interest.

A Tartar or Arabian chief draws his revenue from profit. It comes mainly from the milk and the natural increase of his own herds and flocks, which he manages personally, acting as the principal shepherd or herdsman of his own horde or tribe. But it is only in this earliest and crudest stage of civil government that profit has ever made up the main part of a monarchy's public revenue.

Small republics have sometimes drawn a substantial revenue from commercial ventures. The republic of Hamburg is said to do so from the profits of a public wine-cellar and apothecary's shop. (See Memoires concernant les Droits et Impositions en Europe, volume i, page 73. This work was compiled by order of the court for a commission that had spent several years considering how best to reform the finances of France. The account of the French taxes, which fills three quarto volumes, can be regarded as perfectly authentic. The account of the taxes of other European nations was put together from whatever information the French ministers at the various courts could obtain; it is much shorter and probably not quite as exact as the account of the French taxes.) Any state must be quite small if its sovereign has the spare time to run the business of a wine-merchant or an apothecary. The profit of a public bank has been a source of revenue to more considerable states. This was true not only of Hamburg but of Venice and Amsterdam. Some people have even thought a revenue of this kind worthy of an empire as great as Great Britain. If you reckon the ordinary dividend of the Bank of England at five and a half per cent and its capital at ten million seven hundred and eighty thousand pounds, the net annual profit, after paying for management, is said to come to five hundred and ninety-two thousand nine hundred pounds. Government, it is claimed, could borrow this capital at three per cent interest and, by taking the bank's management into its own hands, could clear a profit of two hundred and sixty-nine thousand five hundred pounds a year. Experience shows that the orderly, watchful, and frugal administration of aristocracies like those of Venice and Amsterdam is extremely well suited to managing a commercial venture of this kind. But whether a government like England's could be safely trusted with such a project is, at the very least, far more doubtful. Whatever its virtues, England has never been famous for good economy; in peacetime it has generally managed its affairs with the lazy, careless extravagance that is perhaps natural to monarchies, and in wartime it has consistently acted with all the thoughtless extravagance that democracies are prone to.

The post office is really a commercial venture. The government puts up the cost of setting up the various offices and of buying or hiring the necessary horses and carriages, and it is repaid, with a large profit, through the charges on what it carries. It is perhaps the only commercial venture that has been managed successfully by, I believe, every sort of government. The capital required is not very large. There is no mystery to the business. And the returns are not only certain but immediate.

Princes, however, have often gone into many other commercial ventures, willing, like private individuals, to improve their fortunes by becoming adventurers in the ordinary branches of trade. They have almost never succeeded. The extravagance with which a prince's affairs are always run makes success nearly impossible. A prince's agents treat their master's wealth as inexhaustible: they are careless about what price they buy at, careless about what price they sell at, careless about what it costs to ship his goods from one place to another. These agents often live with a prince's extravagance, and sometimes, in spite of that extravagance and by a clever way of keeping their accounts, they end up acquiring a prince's fortune. According to Machiavelli, this is exactly how the agents of Lorenzo de' Medici, no prince of mean abilities, ran his trade. The republic of Florence was several times forced to pay off the debts their extravagance had run up for him. So he found it convenient to give up the merchant's business, the very business to which his family had originally owed their fortune, and in the later part of his life to spend what was left of that fortune, together with the state revenue he controlled, on projects and expenses more befitting his rank.

No two roles seem more at odds than those of trader and sovereign. If the trading mentality of the English East India Company makes them very bad sovereigns, the sovereign mentality seems to have made them equally bad traders. While they were only traders they managed their trade successfully and could pay their stockholders a moderate dividend out of the profits. Since they became sovereigns, with a revenue said to have started at more than three million sterling, they have had to beg the ordinary assistance of government to avoid immediate bankruptcy. In their earlier situation their servants in India saw themselves as the clerks of merchants; in their present situation those servants see themselves as the ministers of sovereigns.

A state can sometimes draw part of its public revenue from interest on money as well as from the profits of capital. If it has built up a treasure, it can lend part of that treasure either to foreign states or to its own subjects.

The canton of Berne draws a substantial revenue by lending part of its treasure to foreign states, that is, by investing it in the public funds of the various indebted nations of Europe, chiefly those of France and England. The security of this revenue must depend, first, on the security of the funds it is placed in, or on the good faith of the government that manages them; and second, on the certainty or likelihood that peace with the debtor nation will continue. In a war, the debtor nation's very first hostile act might be to cancel the funds it owes. So far as I know, this policy of lending money to foreign states is unique to the canton of Berne.

The city of Hamburg (see Memoire concernant les Droites et Impositions en Europe, volume i, page 73) has set up a kind of public pawn-shop that lends money to the state's subjects on pledges at six per cent interest. This pawn-shop, or lombard as it is called, is claimed to bring the state a revenue of a hundred and fifty thousand crowns, which, at four shillings and sixpence to the crown, comes to £33,750 sterling.

The government of Pennsylvania, without building up any treasure at all, devised a way of lending its subjects not money exactly, but the equivalent of money. It issued paper bills of credit to private individuals at interest, secured on land worth double the loan, to be redeemed fifteen years after their date; in the meantime these bills passed from hand to hand like banknotes, and an act of the assembly made them legal tender in all payments between one inhabitant of the province and another. In this way it raised a moderate revenue that went a long way toward covering an annual expense of about £4,500, the entire ordinary cost of that frugal and orderly government. The success of such a scheme must have depended on three different conditions. First, there had to be a demand for some instrument of commerce besides gold and silver money, or a demand for so much consumable stock that it could not be obtained without sending most of their gold and silver abroad to buy it. Second, the government using the scheme had to have good credit. And third, it had to use the scheme with restraint, never letting the total value of the paper bills exceed the value of the gold and silver money that would otherwise have been needed to keep their trade going. Several other American colonies adopted the same scheme on various occasions; but for lack of this restraint it caused, in most of them, far more disorder than benefit.

Capital and credit, though, are unstable and perishable by nature, which makes them unfit to be relied on as the main funds for the sure, steady, and permanent revenue that alone can give a government security and dignity. No great nation that had advanced beyond the shepherd stage seems ever to have drawn the greater part of its public revenue from such sources.

Land is a fund of a more stable and permanent kind, and so the rent of public lands has been the principal source of public revenue for many a great nation well past the shepherd stage. The ancient republics of Greece and Italy drew most of the revenue that covered the necessary expenses of the commonwealth, for a long time, from the produce or rent of public lands. And the rent of crown lands made up most of the revenue of the ancient sovereigns of Europe for a long time.

War, and preparing for war, are the two things that in modern times account for most of the necessary expense of all great states. But in the ancient republics of Greece and Italy every citizen was a soldier, who both served and trained for service at his own cost. So neither of those two things could put much expense on the state. The rent of a quite modest landed estate could fully cover all the other necessary expenses of government.

In the ancient monarchies of Europe, the manners and customs of the day were enough to prepare the bulk of the people for war; and when they took the field, the terms of their feudal tenures required them to be maintained either at their own expense or at that of their immediate lords, without any new charge on the sovereign. Most of the other expenses of government were very modest. The administration of justice, as has been shown, was a source of revenue rather than a cost. The labor of country people for three days before and three days after harvest was reckoned enough to build and maintain all the bridges, highways, and other public works that the country's commerce was thought to require. In those days the sovereign's main expense seems to have been keeping his own family and household. So the officers of his household were the great officers of state. The lord treasurer collected his rents. The lord steward and lord chamberlain looked after the cost of his family. The care of his stables fell to the lord constable and the lord marshal. His houses were all built like castles and seem to have been the chief fortresses he held. The keepers of those houses or castles could be regarded as a kind of military governor. They seem to have been the only military officers it was necessary to keep in peacetime. Under these conditions the rent of a great landed estate could, in ordinary circumstances, cover all the necessary expenses of government quite well.

In most of the civilized monarchies of Europe today, the rent of all the land in the country, even managed as it probably would be if it all belonged to a single owner, would barely match the ordinary revenue the government levies on the people even in peacetime. Take Great Britain. Its ordinary revenue, including not just what is needed to cover the year's current expenses but also the interest on the public debts and the sinking of part of the principal of those debts, comes to more than ten million a year. Yet the land tax, at four shillings in the pound, falls short of two million a year. This so-called land tax is supposed to amount to one-fifth not only of the rent of all the land, but of the rent of all the houses and the interest on all the capital stock of Great Britain, except the part that is either lent to the public or used as farming stock in cultivating land. A very large share of what this tax produces comes from the rent of houses and the interest on capital stock. The land tax of the city of London, for instance, at four shillings in the pound, comes to £123,399 6s 7d; that of the city of Westminster to £63,092 1s 5d; that of the palaces of Whitehall and St James's to £30,754 6s 3d. A set proportion of the land tax is likewise assessed on all the other cities and corporate towns in the kingdom, and it arises almost entirely either from the rent of houses or from what is taken to be the interest on trading and capital stock. So according to the valuation by which Great Britain is rated for the land tax, the whole mass of revenue from the rent of all the lands, the rent of all the houses, and the interest on all the capital stock, except the part either lent to the public or used in cultivating land, comes to no more than ten million sterling a year, the ordinary revenue the government levies on the people even in peacetime. The valuation by which Great Britain is rated for the land tax is no doubt, taking the whole kingdom on average, far below the real value, though in several particular counties and districts it is said to come close to that value. Many people have estimated the rent of the lands alone, excluding houses and the interest on stock, at twenty million; but that estimate is largely guesswork and, I suspect, just as likely to be above the truth as below it. Yet even if the lands of Great Britain, cultivated as they now are, do not yield more than twenty million a year in rent, they could hardly yield half of that, and most likely not a fourth, if they all belonged to a single owner and were left to the careless, costly, and oppressive management of his agents and stewards. The crown lands of Great Britain at present do not yield a fourth of the rent that could probably be drawn from them if they were owned by private individuals. And if the crown lands were more extensive, they would probably be managed even worse.

The revenue that the great body of the people draws from land is proportional not to the rent but to the produce of the land. The whole annual produce of a country's land, apart from what is held back for seed, is either consumed each year by the great body of the people or exchanged for something else that they consume. So whatever holds the produce of the land below what it would otherwise reach holds down the income of the great body of the people even more than it holds down that of the landowners. The rent of land, the share of the produce that goes to the owners, is hardly anywhere in Great Britain reckoned at more than a third of the whole produce. Suppose land that in one state of cultivation yields a revenue of ten million sterling a year would, in another, yield a rent of twenty million; if rent is taken to be a third of the produce in both cases, the owners' revenue would be lower than it might be by only ten million a year, but the revenue of the great body of the people would be lower than it might be by thirty million a year, after deducting only what is needed for seed. And the country's population would be smaller by the number of people that thirty million a year, again setting aside the seed, could support, according to the particular standard of living and spending among the different ranks of people who shared the remainder.

There is at present no civilized state of any kind in Europe that draws most of its public revenue from the rent of lands the state owns. Yet in all the great monarchies of Europe there are still many large tracts of land belonging to the crown. They are generally forest, and sometimes forests where you can travel several miles and scarcely find a single tree, a sheer waste and loss of country in terms of both produce and population. In every great monarchy of Europe, selling the crown lands would raise a very large sum of money; and if that were used to pay off the public debts, it would free from mortgage a far greater revenue than those lands have ever yielded the crown. In countries where land that is highly improved and cultivated, and yields at the time of sale about as much rent as can readily be got from it, commonly sells for thirty years' purchase, the unimproved, uncultivated, low-rented crown lands might well be expected to sell for forty, fifty, or sixty years' purchase. The crown could immediately enjoy the revenue that this high price would redeem from mortgage. And within a few years it would probably enjoy a further revenue. Once the crown lands had become private property, they would, within a few years, become well improved and well cultivated. The growth in their produce would increase the country's population by raising the income and consumption of the people. And the revenue the crown draws from the duties of customs and excise would necessarily grow along with the income and consumption of the people.

The revenue that the crown draws from crown lands in any civilized monarchy, though it appears to cost individuals nothing, in reality costs society more than perhaps any other revenue of equal size that the crown enjoys. In every case it would be in society's interest to replace this revenue to the crown with some other revenue of equal size and to divide the lands among the people, which could probably be done no better than by putting them up for public sale.

Lands kept for pleasure and display, parks, gardens, public walks, and the like, which are everywhere regarded as causes of expense rather than sources of revenue, seem to be the only lands that ought to belong to the crown in a great and civilized monarchy.

Public capital and public lands, then, the two sources of revenue that may belong specifically to the sovereign or commonwealth, are both improper and inadequate funds for covering the necessary expense of any great and civilized state. It follows that most of this expense must be covered by taxes of one kind or another, with the people contributing a part of their own private income to make up a public revenue for the sovereign or commonwealth.
Part II: Taxes

As was shown in the first book of this Inquiry, the private revenue of individuals comes ultimately from three different sources: rent, profit, and wages. Every tax must finally be paid out of one or another of those three sources of revenue, or out of all of them together. I shall try to give the best account I can of, first, those taxes meant to fall on rent; second, those meant to fall on profit; third, those meant to fall on wages; and fourth, those meant to fall on all three sources of private revenue without distinction. Examining each of these four kinds of tax in turn will divide the second part of this chapter into four articles, three of which will need several further subdivisions. As the following review will show, many of these taxes are not finally paid out of the fund or source of revenue they were meant to fall on.
Before I begin examining particular taxes, I must first set out the four following maxims about taxes in general.

1. The subjects of every state ought to contribute toward the support of the government as nearly as possible in proportion to their respective abilities, that is, in proportion to the revenue they each enjoy under the state's protection. For the individuals of a great nation, the expense of government is like the cost of management to the joint tenants of a great estate, who are all bound to contribute in proportion to their respective interests in it. Whether this maxim is observed or neglected is what we mean by the equality or inequality of taxation. Let me note once and for all that every tax which finally falls on only one of the three kinds of revenue mentioned above is necessarily unequal, to the extent that it does not touch the other two. In the following examination of various taxes I shall rarely take much further notice of this sort of inequality; in most cases I shall confine my remarks to the inequality caused by a particular tax falling unequally on the particular sort of private revenue it affects.

2. The tax each individual is bound to pay ought to be certain, not arbitrary. The time of payment, the manner of payment, and the amount to be paid ought all to be clear and plain to the taxpayer and to everyone else. Where this is not so, every person liable to the tax is put more or less at the mercy of the tax-collector, who can either pile the tax higher on any taxpayer he dislikes, or use the threat of doing so to extort some gift or favor for himself. Uncertain taxation encourages the insolence and invites the corruption of a class of men who are naturally unpopular even where they are neither insolent nor corrupt. In taxation, certainty about what each person ought to pay is so important that a very considerable degree of inequality is, I believe the experience of all nations shows, not nearly as great an evil as even a very small degree of uncertainty.

3. Every tax ought to be levied at the time, or in the manner, most likely to be convenient for the taxpayer to pay it. A tax on the rent of land or houses, payable at the same date that such rents are usually paid, is levied when it is most likely to be convenient for the taxpayer, or when he is most likely to have the means to pay. Taxes on consumable goods that are luxuries are all finally paid by the consumer, generally in a way that is very convenient for him. He pays them bit by bit, as he has occasion to buy the goods. And since he is free either to buy them or not, as he pleases, it must be his own fault if he ever suffers any real inconvenience from such taxes.

4. Every tax ought to be designed so as to take out, and to keep out, of the people's pockets as little as possible beyond what it brings into the public treasury. A tax may take out or keep out of the people's pockets far more than it brings into the public treasury in the four following ways. First, levying it may require a large number of officers, whose salaries can eat up most of what the tax produces, and whose extra fees can impose a further tax on the people. Second, it may obstruct the people's industry and discourage them from going into certain branches of business that might give a living and employment to great numbers; while forcing the people to pay, it may thus shrink or even destroy some of the very funds that would let them pay more easily. Third, through the forfeitures and other penalties incurred by those unlucky individuals who try and fail to evade the tax, it may frequently ruin them and so put an end to the benefit the community might have had from the use of their capital. An ill-judged tax offers a great temptation to smuggling, but the penalties for smuggling must rise in proportion to the temptation. The law, contrary to all the ordinary principles of justice, first creates the temptation and then punishes those who give in to it; and it commonly raises the punishment, too, in proportion to the very circumstance that ought certainly to lessen it, namely the temptation to commit the crime. (See Sketches of the History of Man, page 474 and following.) Fourth, by subjecting the people to the frequent visits and the hateful scrutiny of the tax-collectors, it may expose them to much needless trouble, vexation, and oppression; and though vexation is not, strictly speaking, an expense, it is certainly the equivalent of the expense at which any man would gladly buy himself free of it. It is in one or another of these four ways that taxes are often far more burdensome to the people than they are beneficial to the sovereign.

The obvious justice and usefulness of these maxims have commended them, more or less, to the attention of all nations. Every nation has tried, as best it could judge, to make its taxes as equal as it could contrive; as certain; as convenient to the taxpayer in both the time and the manner of payment; and, in proportion to the revenue they brought the prince, as little burdensome to the people. The short review that follows, of some of the principal taxes used in different ages and countries, will show that the efforts of all nations have not been equally successful in this.
Article I. Taxes upon Rent. Taxes upon the Rent of Land.

A tax on the rent of land can be imposed in one of two ways. It may follow a fixed rule, each district being valued at a certain rent that is not afterward to be changed; or it may be set up to vary with every change in the real rent of the land, rising or falling as cultivation improves or declines.

A land tax that, like Great Britain's, is assessed on each district according to a certain fixed rule, even if it is equal when first set up, must in time become unequal, as different parts of the country are cultivated to unequal degrees of improvement or neglect. In England, the valuation by which the various counties and parishes were assessed for the land tax under the act of the fourth year of William and Mary was very unequal even at its first establishment. To that extent, then, this tax offends against the first of the four maxims above. It conforms perfectly to the other three. It is perfectly certain. The time of payment, being the same as that for the rent, is as convenient as it can be for the taxpayer. Though the landlord is in every case the real taxpayer, the tax is commonly advanced by the tenant, who is then allowed to deduct it from the rent he pays the landlord. This tax is collected by a far smaller number of officers than any other yielding roughly the same revenue. Since the tax on each district does not rise as the rent rises, the sovereign does not share in the profits of the landlord's improvements. Those improvements do sometimes help relieve the other landlords of the district. But the extra tax this may occasionally throw on a particular estate is always so very small that it can never discourage such improvements, nor hold the produce of the land below what it would otherwise reach. Since it has no tendency to reduce the quantity, it can have none to raise the price of that produce. It does not obstruct the people's industry, and it subjects the landlord to no inconvenience besides the unavoidable one of paying the tax. The advantage the landlord has gained from the unchanging fixity of the valuation by which all the lands of Great Britain are rated for the land tax, however, has been due mainly to some circumstances entirely outside the nature of the tax itself.

It has been due partly to the great prosperity of almost every part of the country, the rents of nearly all the estates of Great Britain having risen continually since this valuation was first set, with scarcely any of them falling. So the landlords have almost all gained the difference between the tax they would have paid according to the present rent of their estates and the tax they actually pay according to the old valuation. Had the state of the country been different, with rents gradually falling as cultivation declined, the landlords would almost all have lost this difference instead. Given the way things have actually gone since the Revolution, the fixity of the valuation has helped the landlord and hurt the sovereign. In a different state of things it might have helped the sovereign and hurt the landlord.

Since the tax is payable in money, the valuation of the land is also expressed in money. Since this valuation was established, the value of silver has been fairly steady, and there has been no change in the standard of the coin in either weight or fineness. Had silver risen considerably in value, as it seems to have done over the two centuries before the discovery of the American mines, the fixity of the valuation might have proved very oppressive to the landlord. Had silver fallen considerably in value, as it certainly did for about a century at least after the discovery of those mines, the same fixity of valuation would have greatly reduced this branch of the sovereign's revenue. And had any significant change been made in the standard of the money, either by sinking the same quantity of silver to a lower denomination or raising it to a higher one, the effect would have been one-sided. If an ounce of silver, for example, instead of being coined into five shillings and twopence, had been coined into pieces with a denomination as low as two shillings and sevenpence, or as high as ten shillings and fourpence, it would in the one case have hurt the owner's revenue and in the other the sovereign's.

In circumstances, then, somewhat different from those that have actually occurred, this fixity of valuation might have been a very great inconvenience either to the taxpayers or to the commonwealth. And over the course of ages such circumstances must sooner or later arise. Empires, like all the other works of men, have so far all proved mortal, yet every empire aims at immortality. Every constitution, therefore, that is meant to be as lasting as the empire itself ought to be convenient not in certain circumstances only, but in all; it ought to suit not the circumstances that are passing, occasional, or accidental, but those that are necessary and therefore always the same.

A tax on the rent of land that varies with every change in the rent, rising and falling as cultivation improves or is neglected, is recommended as the most equitable of all taxes by that school of writers in France who call themselves the economists. All taxes, they claim, fall ultimately on the rent of land and ought therefore to be imposed equally on the fund that must finally pay them. That all taxes ought to fall as equally as possible on the fund that must finally pay them is certainly true. But without getting into the tiresome discussion of the metaphysical arguments by which they support their very ingenious theory, the following review will make sufficiently clear which taxes fall finally on the rent of land and which fall finally on some other fund.

In the Venetian territory, all arable lands leased to farmers are taxed at a tenth of the rent. (Memoires concernant les Droits, pages 240, 241.) The leases are entered in a public register kept by the revenue officers in each province or district. When the owner cultivates his own lands, they are valued by a fair estimate, and he is allowed to deduct one-fifth of the tax, so that for such land he pays only eight rather than ten per cent of the supposed rent.

A land tax of this kind is certainly more equal than the land tax of England. It might not, perhaps, be quite as certain, and assessing the tax might often cause the landlord a good deal more trouble. It might also be a good deal more expensive to collect.
A system of administration could perhaps be devised, however, that would largely both prevent this uncertainty and keep this expense moderate.

For example, the landlord and tenant might be jointly required to enter their lease in a public register. Proper penalties could be set for concealing or misrepresenting any of the terms; and if part of those penalties went to whichever of the two parties informed against and convicted the other of such concealment or misrepresentation, it would effectively stop them from colluding to defraud the public revenue. All the terms of the lease could then be sufficiently known from the record.

Some landlords, instead of raising the rent, take a lump-sum fee for renewing the lease. In most cases this practice is the resort of a spendthrift who, for a sum of ready money, sells off a future income of much greater value. So in most cases it hurts the landlord; it frequently hurts the tenant; and it always hurts the community. It often takes so large a part of the tenant's capital, and so reduces his ability to cultivate the land, that he finds it harder to pay a small rent than he would otherwise have found it to pay a large one. Whatever lowers his ability to cultivate necessarily holds down, below what it would otherwise be, the most important part of the community's revenue. By making the tax on such fees a good deal heavier than the tax on ordinary rent, this harmful practice could be discouraged, to the considerable benefit of all the parties involved: the landlord, the tenant, the sovereign, and the whole community.

Some leases require the tenant to follow a certain mode of cultivation and a certain rotation of crops throughout the whole term of the lease. This condition, which generally springs from the landlord's conceit of his own superior knowledge (a conceit in most cases very ill-founded), ought always to be treated as an extra rent, a rent paid in service rather than in money. To discourage the practice, which is usually a foolish one, this kind of rent might be valued rather high and consequently taxed somewhat higher than ordinary money rents.

Some landlords, instead of a rent in money, require a rent in kind, in corn, cattle, poultry, wine, oil, and so on; others again require a rent in service. Such rents always hurt the tenant more than they benefit the landlord. They either take more, or keep more, out of the tenant's pocket than they put into the landlord's. In every country where they occur, the tenants are poor and wretched, more or less in proportion to how widespread these rents are. By valuing such rents rather high in the same way, and consequently taxing them somewhat higher than ordinary money rents, a practice harmful to the whole community might perhaps be sufficiently discouraged.

When the landlord chose to occupy part of his own lands himself, the rent might be valued by a fair arbitration among the neighboring farmers and landlords, and he might be granted a moderate reduction of the tax, just as in the Venetian territory, provided the rent of the lands he occupied did not exceed a certain sum. It is important that the landlord should be encouraged to cultivate part of his own land. His capital is generally greater than the tenant's, and with less skill he can often raise a greater produce. The landlord can afford to try experiments and is generally inclined to do so. His failed experiments cost him only a moderate loss. His successful ones contribute to the improvement and better cultivation of the whole country. It might be important, though, that the tax reduction encourage him to cultivate only up to a point. If most landlords were tempted to farm the whole of their own lands, the country, instead of having sober and hardworking tenants bound by their own interest to cultivate as well as their capital and skill allow, would be filled with idle and dissolute bailiffs, whose abusive management would soon degrade the cultivation and reduce the annual produce of the land, to the loss not only of their masters' revenue but of the most important part of the revenue of the whole society.

Such a system of administration might perhaps free a tax of this kind from any uncertainty that could cause oppression or inconvenience to the taxpayer; and it might at the same time help introduce into the ordinary management of land a policy that would contribute a good deal to the general improvement and good cultivation of the country.

The cost of collecting a land tax that varied with every change in the rent would no doubt be somewhat greater than that of collecting one always rated by a fixed valuation. Some extra expense would necessarily arise, both from the various register-offices it would be proper to set up in the different districts of the country and from the various valuations occasionally made of the lands the owner chose to occupy himself. But the cost of all this might be very moderate, and far below what is incurred in collecting many other taxes that yield a very small revenue compared with what could easily be drawn from a tax of this kind.

The discouragement that a variable land tax of this kind might give to the improvement of land seems to be the most important objection that can be raised against it. The landlord would certainly be less inclined to improve when the sovereign, who contributed nothing to the cost, was to share in the profit of the improvement. Even this objection might perhaps be met, by allowing the landlord, before beginning his improvement, to fix, together with the revenue officers, the actual value of his lands by a fair arbitration of a certain number of neighboring landlords and farmers, equally chosen by both sides, and then to be rated according to that valuation for as many years as would fully repay his outlay. One of the main advantages claimed for this kind of land tax is that it draws the sovereign's attention toward the improvement of the land, out of regard for the increase of his own revenue. So the term allowed for the landlord's repayment ought not to be much longer than necessary for that purpose, lest the remoteness of the interest discourage this attention too much. Even so, it had better be somewhat too long than in any way too short. No incentive to the sovereign's attention can ever outweigh the smallest discouragement to the landlord's. The sovereign's attention can at best be only a very general and vague consideration of what is likely to improve the cultivation of most of his dominions. The landlord's attention is a particular and minute consideration of how every inch of ground on his estate may be put to best use. The sovereign's chief concern ought to be to encourage, by every means in his power, the attention of both landlord and farmer: by letting both pursue their own interest in their own way and according to their own judgment; by giving both the fullest security that they shall enjoy the complete reward of their own industry; and by securing both the widest market for every part of their produce, through establishing the easiest and safest communications by both land and water throughout his own dominions, as well as the most unbounded freedom to export to the dominions of all other princes.

If, by such a system of administration, a tax of this kind could be managed so as to give the improvement of land not only no discouragement but on the contrary some encouragement, it does not seem likely to cause the landlord any inconvenience other than the unavoidable one of having to pay the tax. Through all the changes in the state of society, in the advance and the decline of agriculture, through all the changes in the value of silver and in the standard of the coin, a tax of this kind would, of its own accord and without any attention from government, readily adjust itself to the actual state of things, and would be equally just and equitable through all those different changes. It would therefore be far more suitable to be established as a permanent and unalterable regulation, or as what is called a fundamental law of the commonwealth, than any tax always to be levied according to a certain valuation.

Some states, instead of the simple and obvious expedient of a register of leases, have resorted to the laborious and expensive one of an actual survey and valuation of all the lands in the country. They have probably suspected that the lessor and lessee, in order to defraud the public revenue, might collude to conceal the real terms of the lease. The Domesday Book seems to have been the result of a very accurate survey of this kind.

In the ancient dominions of the king of Prussia, the land tax is assessed by an actual survey and valuation, which is reviewed and revised from time to time. (Memoires concernant les Droits, etc., volume i, pages 114, 115, 116, etc.) According to that valuation, lay proprietors pay from twenty to twenty-five per cent of their revenue, and clergy from forty to forty-five per cent. The survey and valuation of Silesia was made, it is said, with great accuracy by order of the present king. According to it, the lands belonging to the bishop of Breslau are taxed at twenty-five per cent of their rent; the other revenues of the clergy of both religions at fifty per cent; the commanderies of the Teutonic order and of the order of Malta at forty per cent; lands held by a noble tenure at thirty-eight and one-third per cent; and lands held by a base tenure at thirty-five and one-third per cent.

The survey and valuation of Bohemia is said to have taken more than a hundred years' work. It was not completed until after the peace of 1748, by order of the present empress queen. (Same work, volume i, pages 85, 84.) The survey of the duchy of Milan, begun in the time of Charles VI, was not completed until after 1760. It is reckoned one of the most accurate ever made. The survey of Savoy and Piedmont was carried out by order of the late king of Sardinia. (Same work, page 280, etc.; also pages 287 to 316.)

In the dominions of the king of Prussia, the revenue of the church is taxed much higher than that of lay proprietors. Most of the revenue of the church is a burden on the rent of land. It seldom happens that any of it is put toward improving land, or used in any way that helps increase the revenue of the great body of the people. The king of Prussia had probably for that reason thought it reasonable that it should contribute a good deal more toward meeting the needs of the state. In some countries the lands of the church are exempt from all taxes. In others they are taxed more lightly than other lands. In the duchy of Milan, the lands the church held before 1575 are rated for the tax at only a third of their value.

In Silesia, lands held by a noble tenure are taxed three per cent higher than those held by a base tenure. The king of Prussia had probably reckoned that the honors and privileges of various kinds attached to the noble tenure would adequately compensate the owner for a small increase in the tax, while at the same time the humiliating inferiority of the base tenure would be somewhat softened by being taxed a little more lightly. In other countries the system of taxation aggravates this inequality instead of softening it. In the dominions of the king of Sardinia, and in those provinces of France subject to what is called the real or predial taille, the tax falls entirely on lands held by a base tenure. Those held by a noble tenure are exempt.

A land tax assessed by a general survey and valuation, however equal it may be at first, must within quite a moderate period of time become unequal. To keep it from doing so would demand the continual and painful attention of government to all the changes in the state and produce of every different farm in the country. The governments of Prussia, Bohemia, Sardinia, and the duchy of Milan do in fact exert an attention of this kind, an attention so ill-suited to the nature of government that it is unlikely to last long, and which, if it does last, will probably in the long run cause far more trouble and vexation than any relief it can bring the taxpayers.

In 1666, the generality of Montauban was assessed for the real or predial taille according, it is said, to a very exact survey and valuation. (Memoires concernant les Droits, etc., volume ii, page 139, etc.) By 1727 this assessment had become thoroughly unequal. To remedy the problem, the government found no better expedient than to impose on the whole generality an extra tax of a hundred and twenty thousand livres. This extra tax is rated on all the different districts subject to the taille according to the old assessment. But it is collected only from those districts that, as things actually stand, are under-taxed by that assessment, and it is applied to relieve those that are over-taxed by it. Take two districts, for example, one of which ought, as things actually stand, to be taxed at nine hundred livres and the other at eleven hundred, but which the old assessment taxes both at a thousand. Under the extra tax, both districts are rated at eleven hundred livres each. But the extra tax is collected only from the under-charged district, and it is applied entirely to relieve the over-charged one, which consequently pays only nine hundred livres. The government neither gains nor loses by the extra tax, which goes entirely to correcting the inequalities arising from the old assessment. How it is applied is largely left to the discretion of the intendant of the generality and must therefore be in great measure arbitrary.
Taxes Proportioned Not to the Rent, but to the Produce of Land

Taxes on the produce of land are really taxes on the rent; and although the farmer may originally advance them, they are finally paid by the landlord. When a certain portion of the produce has to be handed over for a tax, the farmer reckons as best he can what that portion is likely to be worth, one year with another, and makes a corresponding reduction in the rent he agrees to pay the landlord. There is no farmer who does not work out in advance what the church tithe, which is a land tax of this kind, is likely to come to, one year with another.

The tithe, and every other land tax of this sort, looks perfectly even-handed but is in fact deeply unequal, because the same share of the produce amounts to very different shares of the rent depending on the land. On some very rich land the harvest is so large that half of it is enough to cover the farmer's working capital along with the ordinary profit on farming stock in the neighbourhood. The other half—or, what comes to the same thing, the value of the other half—he could afford to hand over as rent to the landlord if there were no tithe. But if a tenth of the produce is taken from him as tithe, he has to demand that his rent be cut by a fifth, or he cannot recover his capital with the ordinary profit. In that case the landlord's rent, instead of being a half, or five-tenths of the whole produce, comes to only four-tenths. On poorer land it is the reverse: the harvest is sometimes so small, and cultivation so costly, that four-fifths of the whole produce is needed just to replace the farmer's capital with the ordinary profit. Here, even without any tithe, the landlord's rent could be no more than a fifth, or two-tenths, of the whole produce. And if the farmer pays a tenth of the produce as tithe, he must demand an equal reduction in the landlord's rent, which is therefore cut to just a tenth of the whole produce. So on rich land the tithe may sometimes be a tax of no more than a fifth, or four shillings in the pound; whereas on poorer land it may sometimes be a tax of a half, or ten shillings in the pound.

Because the tithe is often such an uneven tax on rent, it is also always a serious deterrent both to improvement by the landlord and to cultivation by the farmer. The landlord dares not undertake the most important improvements, which are usually the most expensive, and the farmer dares not raise the most valuable crops, which are usually the most expensive too, when the church—which pays none of the cost—is going to take so large a share of the profit. For a long time the growing of madder was confined to the United Provinces, which, being Presbyterian countries and therefore exempt from this destructive tax, enjoyed a kind of monopoly over that useful dyeing drug against the rest of Europe. The recent attempts to introduce the crop into England have only come about because of the statute providing that five shillings an acre be accepted in place of every kind of tithe on madder.

Just as the church is supported mainly by a land tax across most of Europe, so in many countries of Asia the state is supported mainly by a land tax—one geared not to the rent but to the produce of the land. In China the sovereign's chief revenue is a tenth of the produce of all the empire's lands. This tenth, however, is assessed so modestly that in many provinces it is said not to exceed a thirtieth of the ordinary produce. The land tax, or land rent, that used to be paid to the Mohammedan government of Bengal before that country fell into the hands of the English East India Company is said to have come to about a fifth of the produce. The land tax of ancient Egypt is likewise said to have come to a fifth.

In Asia this kind of land tax is said to give the sovereign a stake in improving and cultivating the land. The rulers of China, those of Bengal under the Mohammedan government, and those of ancient Egypt were accordingly said to be extremely attentive to building and maintaining good roads and navigable canals, so as to increase as much as possible both the quantity and the value of every part of the land's produce, by giving every part the widest market their own dominions could supply. The church's tithe, by contrast, is split into such small portions that no single owner of it has any interest of this kind. The parson of a parish could never see any benefit in building a road or canal to a distant part of the country in order to widen the market for his own parish's produce. Such taxes, when meant for the upkeep of the state, have certain advantages that may to some degree offset their drawbacks. When meant for the upkeep of the church, they bring nothing but drawbacks.
Taxes on the produce of land may be collected either in kind or according to a set valuation in money.

The parson of a parish, or a gentleman of small fortune who lives on his estate, may sometimes find it worthwhile to receive payment in kind—the one his tithe, the other his rent. The amount to be gathered and the district it is gathered in are both so small that each man can oversee with his own eyes the collection and disposal of everything owed to him. A gentleman of great fortune living in the capital, however, would be liable to lose a great deal through the negligence, and still more through the fraud, of his stewards and agents if the rents of an estate in a distant province were paid to him this way. The sovereign's loss from the abuse and plundering of his tax-gatherers would necessarily be far greater. The servants of even the most careless private person are probably more closely watched by their master than those of the most careful prince; and a public revenue paid in kind would suffer so much from the mismanagement of the collectors that only a very small part of what was taken from the people would ever reach the prince's treasury. Some part of China's public revenue, however, is said to be paid this way. The mandarins and other tax-gatherers no doubt find it to their advantage to keep up a form of payment that is so much more open to abuse than any payment in money.

A tax on the produce of land that is collected in money may be charged either by a valuation that shifts with every movement of the market price, or by a fixed valuation—for example, a bushel of wheat always reckoned at one and the same money price, whatever the market may be doing. The yield of a tax charged the first way will vary only with changes in the land's actual produce, according to whether cultivation improves or declines. The yield of a tax charged the second way will vary not only with changes in the land's produce, but also with changes in the value of the precious metals and with changes in how much of those metals is contained at different times in coin of the same denomination. The first will always bear the same proportion to the value of the land's real produce. The second may at different times bear very different proportions to that value.

When, instead of either a fixed share of the land's produce or the price of a fixed share, a set sum of money is to be paid in full settlement of all tax or tithe, the tax becomes exactly the same in nature as the land tax of England. It neither rises nor falls with the rent of the land. It neither encourages nor discourages improvement. The tithe in most of those parishes that pay what is called a modus, in place of all other tithe, is a tax of this kind. During the Mohammedan government of Bengal, a modus—and, it is said, a very moderate one—was set up in most of the districts or zemindaries of the country in place of paying a fifth of the produce in kind. Some of the East India Company's servants, on the pretext of restoring the public revenue to its proper value, have in some provinces swapped this modus for a payment in kind. Under their management this change is likely both to discourage cultivation and to open new opportunities for abuse in collecting the public revenue, which has fallen far below what it was said to be when it first came under the Company's management. The Company's servants may perhaps have gained from the change, but probably at the expense both of their masters and of the country.
Taxes on the Rent of Houses.
The rent of a house can be split into two parts. One may quite properly be called the building-rent; the other is usually called the ground-rent.

The building-rent is the interest or profit on the capital spent in putting up the house. For the builder's trade to be on a par with other trades, this rent has to be enough, first, to give him the same interest he would have earned on his capital had he lent it out on good security, and second, to keep the house in constant repair—or, what amounts to the same thing, to replace, within a certain number of years, the capital that went into building it. The building-rent, or the ordinary profit of building, is therefore everywhere governed by the ordinary interest on money. Where the market rate of interest is four per cent, a house that, on top of paying the ground-rent, yields six or six and a half per cent on the whole cost of building may perhaps give the builder a sufficient profit. Where the market rate of interest is five per cent, it may take seven or seven and a half per cent. If, relative to the interest on money, the building trade ever yields much greater profit than this, it will soon pull enough capital from other trades to bring the profit back down to its proper level. If it ever yields much less, other trades will soon pull enough capital out of it to raise that profit again.

Whatever part of a house's whole rent is over and above what is needed to give this reasonable profit naturally goes to the ground-rent; and where the owner of the ground and the owner of the building are two different people, it is in most cases paid in full to the former. This surplus rent is the price the occupant pays for some real or supposed advantage of the location. In country houses far from any large town, where there is plenty of ground to choose from, the ground-rent is next to nothing—no more than what the ground the house stands on would pay if used for farming. In country villas near a large town it is sometimes a good deal higher, and the particular convenience or beauty of the spot is often very well paid for. Ground-rents are generally highest in the capital, and in those particular parts of it where demand for houses happens to be greatest, whatever the reason for that demand—whether trade and business, pleasure and society, or mere vanity and fashion.

A tax on house-rent, payable by the tenant and set in proportion to the whole rent of each house, could not, at least for any length of time, fall on the building-rent. If the builder did not get his reasonable profit, he would have to leave the trade; and that, by raising the demand for building, would soon bring his profit back to its proper level with the other trades. Nor would such a tax fall entirely on the ground-rent. Instead it would divide itself so as to fall partly on the occupant of the house and partly on the owner of the ground.

Suppose, for example, that a particular person decides he can afford to spend a total of sixty pounds a year on house-rent, and suppose too that a tax of four shillings in the pound, or a fifth, payable by the occupant, is laid on house-rent. A house with a sixty-pound rent would then cost him seventy-two pounds a year, which is twelve pounds more than he thinks he can afford. So he will settle for a worse house, one with a fifty-pound rent, which, with the extra ten pounds he must pay in tax, comes to the sixty pounds a year he reckons he can manage; and to pay the tax he gives up part of the extra comfort he might have had from a house renting for ten pounds more. I say part of that extra comfort, because he will rarely have to give up all of it: thanks to the tax he gets a better house for fifty pounds a year than he could have had without the tax. By removing this particular competitor, a tax of this kind cuts the competition for sixty-pound houses, and likewise cuts it for fifty-pound houses, and in the same way for houses of every other rent—except the lowest, where for a time it would actually increase the competition. But the rents of every class of house for which competition fell would necessarily be reduced more or less. Since none of this reduction could, at least for any length of time, fall on the building-rent, all of it must in the long run fall on the ground-rent. So the final payment of this tax would fall partly on the occupant of the house, who to pay his share must give up some of his comfort, and partly on the owner of the ground, who to pay his share must give up some of his revenue. In what proportion this final payment would be split between them is perhaps not very easy to determine. The division would probably be very different in different circumstances, and a tax of this kind might, depending on those circumstances, fall very unequally on both the occupant of the house and the owner of the ground.

Any unevenness with which a tax of this kind fell on the owners of different ground-rents would arise entirely from the chance unevenness of this division. But the unevenness with which it fell on the occupants of different houses would arise not only from this but from another cause as well. The share of house-rent in total living expenses differs at different levels of wealth. It is perhaps highest at the highest level, and falls gradually through the lower levels, so as to be generally lowest at the lowest. For the poor, the necessities of life make up the great expense. They find it hard to get food, and most of their small income goes on getting it. For the rich, the luxuries and vanities of life make up the chief expense; and a magnificent house shows off all their other luxuries and vanities to the best advantage. A tax on house-rents would therefore generally fall heaviest on the rich, and in this kind of unevenness there is perhaps nothing very unreasonable. It is not very unreasonable that the rich should contribute to public expense not merely in proportion to their revenue, but somewhat more than in that proportion.

The rent of houses, although in some ways it resembles the rent of land, differs from it in one essential respect. The rent of land is paid for the use of something productive. The land that pays the rent also produces it. The rent of houses is paid for the use of something unproductive. Neither the house nor the ground it stands on produces anything. So the person who pays the rent must draw it from some other source of revenue, separate from and independent of the house itself. A tax on house-rent, so far as it falls on the occupants, must be drawn from the same source as the rent itself, and must be paid out of their revenue, whether that comes from the wages of labour, the profits of stock, or the rent of land. So far as it falls on the occupants, it is one of those taxes that fall not on one source of revenue alone but indifferently on all three; and it is in every respect the same in nature as a tax on any other consumable commodity. In general there is perhaps no single item of expense or consumption that better reveals how generous or how stingy a man's whole spending is than his house-rent. A proportional tax on this particular item might perhaps yield a more considerable revenue than any drawn from it so far in any part of Europe. If the tax were very high, though, most people would try to dodge it as much as they could by making do with smaller houses and shifting much of their spending into some other channel.

The rent of houses could be worked out accurately enough by a method of the same kind needed to work out the ordinary rent of land. Uninhabited houses should pay no tax. A tax on them would fall entirely on the owner, who would then be taxed for something that gave him neither comfort nor revenue. Houses lived in by their owner should be rated not by what they cost to build but by the rent a fair arbitration judges they would likely fetch if leased to a tenant. Rated by their building cost, a tax of three or four shillings in the pound, on top of other taxes, would ruin almost all the rich and great families of this country, and I believe of every other civilized country. Anyone who examines carefully the various town and country houses of some of the richest and greatest families here will find that, at a rate of only six and a half or seven per cent on the original building cost, their house-rent nearly equals the whole net rent of their estates. It is the accumulated spending of several generations, laid out on objects of great beauty and magnificence, yet of very small exchangeable value in proportion to what they cost. {Since this book was first published, a tax along roughly the principles described above has been imposed.}

Ground-rents are an even more suitable subject for taxation than the rent of houses. A tax on ground-rents would not raise the rent of houses; it would fall entirely on the owner of the ground-rent, who always behaves as a monopolist and charges the greatest rent he can get for the use of his ground. More or less can be got for it depending on whether the competitors happen to be richer or poorer, or can afford to indulge their fancy for a particular spot at greater or lesser expense. In every country the greatest number of rich competitors is in the capital, and that is accordingly where the highest ground-rents are always found. Since a tax on ground-rents would do nothing to increase those competitors' wealth, they probably would not be willing to pay more for the use of the ground. Whether the tax was advanced by the occupant or by the owner of the ground would make little difference. The more the occupant had to pay in tax, the less he would be willing to pay for the ground, so the final payment of the tax would fall entirely on the owner of the ground-rent. The ground-rents of uninhabited houses should pay no tax. Both ground-rents and the ordinary rent of land are a kind of revenue that the owner in many cases enjoys without any care or effort of his own. Even if part of this revenue is taken from him to meet the expenses of the state, no discouragement is thereby given to any kind of industry. The yearly produce of the society's land and labour—the real wealth and revenue of the great body of the people—could be the same after such a tax as before. Ground-rents and the ordinary rent of land are therefore perhaps the kinds of revenue best able to bear a special tax laid on them.

In this respect ground-rents seem an even more suitable subject for special taxation than the ordinary rent of land. The ordinary rent of land is in many cases owing, at least in part, to the landlord's attention and good management. A very heavy tax might discourage that attention and good management too much. Ground-rents, so far as they exceed the ordinary rent of land, are owing entirely to the good government of the sovereign, which, by protecting the industry of either the whole people or the inhabitants of a particular place, lets them pay so much more than the real value for the ground they build on, or makes their use of the ground more than worth the owner's while. Nothing could be more reasonable than that a fund which owes its very existence to the good government of the state should be taxed in a special way, or should contribute something more than most other funds towards supporting that government.

Although taxes on house-rent have been imposed in many countries of Europe, I know of none in which ground-rents have been treated as a separate subject of taxation. Those who devise taxes have probably found some difficulty in deciding what part of the rent should count as ground-rent and what part as building-rent. Yet it should not be very hard to tell these two parts of the rent apart.

In Great Britain the rent of houses is supposed to be taxed in the same proportion as the rent of land, through what is called the annual land tax. The valuation by which each parish and district is assessed for this tax is always the same. It was extremely uneven to begin with, and it remains so. Across most of the kingdom this tax falls even more lightly on the rent of houses than on that of land. Only in a few districts, originally rated high and where the rent of houses has since fallen a good deal, is the land tax of three or four shillings in the pound said to amount to an equal proportion of the real rent of houses. Untenanted houses, though by law liable to the tax, are in most districts let off by the favour of the assessors; and this exemption sometimes causes some small variation in the rate on particular houses, even though the rate of the district is always the same. Increases in rent through new buildings, repairs, and the like go to relieve the district's total, which causes still further variations in the rate on particular houses.

In the province of Holland {Memoires concernant les Droits, etc. p. 223.}, every house is taxed at two and a half per cent of its value, with no regard either to the rent it actually brings in or to whether it is tenanted or untenanted. There seems to be a hardship in forcing the owner to pay a tax for an untenanted house from which he can draw no revenue—especially so heavy a tax. In Holland, where the market rate of interest does not exceed three per cent, two and a half per cent on the whole value of a house must in most cases come to more than a third of the building-rent, perhaps of the whole rent. The valuation by which the houses are rated, though very uneven, is said to be always below the real value. When a house is rebuilt, improved, or enlarged, there is a fresh valuation and the tax is rated accordingly.

Those who devised the various taxes laid on houses at different times in England seem to have imagined there was some great difficulty in establishing, with tolerable accuracy, the real rent of every house. So they geared their taxes to some more obvious circumstance that they probably supposed would in most cases bear some proportion to the rent.

The first tax of this kind was hearth-money, a tax of two shillings on every hearth. To find out how many hearths a house had, the tax-gatherer had to enter every room. This hateful visit made the tax hateful, and so, soon after the Revolution, it was abolished as a badge of slavery.

The next tax of this kind was a tax of two shillings on every inhabited dwelling-house, with a house of ten windows paying four shillings more, and a house of twenty windows and upwards paying eight shillings. The tax was later altered so that houses with twenty to fewer than thirty windows paid ten shillings, and those with thirty windows and upwards paid twenty shillings. In most cases the windows can be counted from outside, and in all cases without entering every room. The tax-gatherer's visit was therefore less offensive with this tax than with the hearth-money.

This tax was later repealed, and in its place came the window-tax, which has since gone through two separate changes and increases. As it stands now (January 1775), on top of a duty of three shillings on every house in England and one shilling on every house in Scotland, the window-tax lays a duty on every window that in England rises gradually from twopence—the lowest rate, on houses with no more than seven windows—to two shillings, the highest rate, on houses with twenty-five windows and upwards.

The main objection to all such taxes is their unevenness—unevenness of the worst kind, since they often fall much more heavily on the poor than on the rich. A house renting for ten pounds in a country town may sometimes have more windows than a house renting for five hundred pounds in London; and although the occupant of the former is likely to be a much poorer man than the occupant of the latter, his contribution, so far as it is set by the window-tax, must be greater. Such taxes therefore run directly counter to the first of the four maxims mentioned above. They do not seem to offend much against any of the other three.

The natural tendency of the window-tax, and of every other tax on houses, is to lower rents. The more a man pays in tax, the less he can clearly afford to pay in rent. Since the window-tax was imposed, however, house rents have on the whole risen, more or less, in almost every town and village of Great Britain I know of. Almost everywhere the demand for houses has grown so much that it has raised rents more than the window-tax could lower them—one of the many proofs of the country's great prosperity and of its inhabitants' growing revenue. Without the tax, rents would probably have risen still higher.
ARTICLE II.—Taxes on Profit, or on the Revenue arising from Stock.

The revenue or profit arising from stock naturally divides into two parts: the part that pays the interest and belongs to the owner of the stock, and the surplus part over and above what is needed to pay the interest.

This second part of profit is clearly not something that can be taxed directly. It is the compensation—and in most cases no more than a very moderate compensation—for the risk and trouble of employing the stock. The employer must have this compensation, or it would be against his own interest to keep up the employment. So if he were taxed directly in proportion to the whole profit, he would have to either raise his rate of profit or charge the tax to the interest on money, that is, pay less interest. If he raised his rate of profit in proportion to the tax, the whole tax, though he might advance it, would finally be paid by one or other of two sets of people, depending on how he employed the stock under his management. If he used it as farming stock, in cultivating land, he could raise his rate of profit only by keeping a larger share, or the price of a larger share, of the land's produce; and since this could only be done by cutting rent, the final payment of the tax would fall on the landlord. If he used it as mercantile or manufacturing stock, he could raise his rate of profit only by raising the price of his goods, in which case the final payment of the tax would fall entirely on the consumers of those goods. If he did not raise his rate of profit, he would have to charge the whole tax to the part of profit set aside for the interest on money. He could afford less interest on whatever stock he borrowed, and the whole weight of the tax would then fall ultimately on the interest of money. To the extent he could not relieve himself of the tax one way, he would have to relieve himself the other.

At first glance the interest of money seems as capable of being taxed directly as the rent of land. Like the rent of land, it is a net produce that remains after fully compensating all the risk and trouble of employing the stock. Just as a tax on the rent of land cannot raise rents—because the net produce left after replacing the farmer's stock and his reasonable profit cannot be greater after the tax than before—so, for the same reason, a tax on the interest of money could not raise the rate of interest, since the quantity of stock or money in the country, like the quantity of land, is assumed to remain the same after the tax as before. As shown in the first book, the ordinary rate of profit is everywhere governed by the quantity of stock to be employed in proportion to the amount of employment, or of business, that must be done by it. But neither the amount of employment nor the business to be done by stock could be increased or decreased by any tax on the interest of money. So if the quantity of stock to be employed was neither increased nor decreased by it, the ordinary rate of profit would necessarily stay the same. The portion of that profit needed to compensate the employer's risk and trouble would likewise stay the same, since that risk and trouble are not altered at all. The remainder, then—the portion belonging to the owner of the stock, which pays the interest of money—would necessarily stay the same too. At first glance, therefore, the interest of money seems as fit to be taxed directly as the rent of land.
There are, however, two distinct circumstances that make the interest of money a much less suitable subject for direct taxation than the rent of land.

First, the quantity and value of the land a man owns can never be hidden and can always be established very exactly. But the whole amount of capital stock he owns is almost always a secret and can hardly ever be established with tolerable exactness. It is also liable to almost constant change. A year rarely passes, often not a month, sometimes hardly a single day, without it rising or falling more or less. An inquiry into every man's private affairs—one that, to fit the tax to those affairs, kept watch over every fluctuation in his fortune—would be a source of such constant and endless harassment that no one could bear it.

Second, land cannot be moved, whereas stock easily can. The owner of land is necessarily a citizen of the particular country where his estate lies. The owner of stock is properly a citizen of the world and is not necessarily tied to any particular country. He would be inclined to abandon a country where he faced a vexatious inquiry in order to be assessed for a burdensome tax, and would move his stock to some other country where he could either carry on his business or enjoy his fortune more at his ease. By moving his stock he would put an end to all the industry it had been supporting in the country he left. Stock cultivates land; stock employs labour. A tax that tended to drive stock out of any particular country would to that extent tend to dry up every source of revenue, both for the sovereign and for the society. Not only the profits of stock, but the rent of land and the wages of labour too, would necessarily be reduced more or less by its removal.

Accordingly, the nations that have tried to tax the revenue arising from stock have, instead of any harsh inquiry of this kind, had to content themselves with a very loose and therefore more or less arbitrary estimate. The extreme unevenness and uncertainty of a tax assessed this way can only be offset by its extreme moderation; and because of that, every man finds himself rated so far below his real revenue that he gives himself little trouble even if his neighbour should be rated somewhat lower.

By what is called the land tax in England, the intention was that stock should be taxed in the same proportion as land. When the tax on land was four shillings in the pound, or a fifth of the supposed rent, the intention was that stock should be taxed at a fifth of the supposed interest. When the present annual land tax was first imposed, the legal rate of interest was six per cent. Every hundred pounds of stock was accordingly supposed to be taxed at twenty-four shillings, a fifth of six pounds. Since the legal rate of interest has been cut to five per cent, every hundred pounds of stock is supposed to be taxed at only twenty shillings. The sum to be raised by the land tax was split between the country and the principal towns. Most of it was laid on the country; and of what was laid on the towns, most was assessed on the houses. What was left to be assessed on the stock or trade of the towns (for the stock employed on the land was not meant to be taxed) was far below the real value of that stock or trade. So whatever unevenness there was in the original assessment caused little trouble. Every parish and district is still rated for its land, its houses, and its stock according to the original assessment; and the almost universal prosperity of the country, which in most places has greatly raised the value of all of these, has made those inequalities of even less importance now. The rate on each district staying always the same has also greatly reduced the uncertainty of this tax as it might be assessed on any individual's stock, as well as making it of much less consequence. If most of the lands of England are not rated for the land tax at half their actual value, most of the stock of England is perhaps scarcely rated at a fiftieth of its actual value. In some towns the whole land tax is assessed on houses—as in Westminster, where stock and trade are free. It is otherwise in London.
In every country a harsh inquiry into the affairs of private persons has been carefully avoided.

At Hamburg {Memoires concernant les Droits, tom. i, p.74}, every inhabitant is required to pay the state one quarter per cent of all he owns; and since the wealth of the people of Hamburg consists mainly in stock, this tax may be regarded as a tax on stock. Each man assesses himself and, in the presence of the magistrate, puts into the public coffer each year a sum of money that he declares on oath to be one quarter per cent of all he owns—without declaring what that amounts to, or being liable to any examination on the matter. This tax is generally supposed to be paid with great honesty. In a small republic, where the people have complete confidence in their magistrates, are convinced the tax is needed to support the state, and believe it will be faithfully applied to that purpose, such conscientious and voluntary payment may sometimes be expected. It is not peculiar to the people of Hamburg.

The canton of Underwald, in Switzerland, is often ravaged by storms and floods, which leave it facing extraordinary expenses. On such occasions the people assemble, and each is said to declare with the greatest frankness what he is worth, so as to be taxed accordingly. At Zurich the law orders that, in cases of necessity, everyone be taxed in proportion to his revenue, the amount of which he must declare on oath. They have no suspicion, it is said, that any of their fellow citizens will deceive them. At Basel the chief revenue of the state comes from a small duty on exported goods. All the citizens swear that they will pay every three months all the taxes the law imposes. All merchants, and even all innkeepers, are trusted to keep their own accounts of the goods they sell, whether inside or outside the territory. At the end of every three months they send this account to the treasurer, with the amount of the tax worked out at the bottom of it. It is not suspected that the revenue suffers from this trust. {Memoires concernant les Droits, tom. i p. 163, 167, 171.}

To require every citizen to declare publicly on oath the amount of his fortune is apparently not reckoned a hardship in those Swiss cantons. At Hamburg it would be reckoned the greatest of hardships. Merchants engaged in the hazardous ventures of trade all dread the thought of being forced, at all times, to lay bare the real state of their affairs.
