The ruin of their credit and the failure of their ventures, they foresee, would too often be the result. A sober and thrifty people, who are strangers to all such ventures, do not feel they have any need for such concealment.

In Holland, soon after the late Prince of Orange was raised to the stadtholdership, a tax of two per cent, or the fiftieth penny as it was called, was imposed on the whole substance of every citizen. Each citizen assessed himself and paid his tax in the same way as at Hamburg, and it was generally supposed to have been paid with great honesty. The people at that time had the greatest affection for their new government, which they had just set up by a general uprising. The tax was to be paid only once, to relieve the state in a particular emergency. It was indeed too heavy to be permanent. In a country where the market rate of interest seldom exceeds three per cent, a tax of two per cent comes to thirteen shillings and fourpence in the pound on the highest net revenue commonly drawn from stock. It is a tax that very few people could pay without eating more or less into their capital. In a particular emergency, the people may from great public zeal make a great effort and give up even part of their capital to relieve the state. But it is impossible for them to keep doing so for any length of time; and if they did, the tax would soon ruin them so completely as to leave them entirely unable to support the state at all.

The tax on stock imposed by the land tax bill in England, though geared to the capital, is not meant to reduce or take away any part of that capital. It is meant only as a tax on the interest of money, geared to the tax on the rent of land, so that when the latter is at four shillings in the pound the former may be at four shillings in the pound too. The tax at Hamburg, and the still more moderate taxes of Underwald and Zurich, are likewise meant as taxes not on the capital but on the interest or net revenue of stock. The Dutch tax was meant as a tax on the capital itself.
Taxes on the Profit of Particular Employments.
In some countries extraordinary taxes are imposed on the profits of stock, sometimes when it is employed in particular branches of trade and sometimes when it is employed in agriculture.

Of the former kind are, in England, the tax on hawkers and pedlars, that on hackney-coaches and chairs, and the one alehouse-keepers pay for a licence to retail ale and spirituous liquors. During the late war another tax of the same kind was proposed on shops. The war, it was said, had been undertaken in defence of the country's trade, so the merchants who were to profit by it ought to contribute towards supporting it.

A tax on the profits of stock employed in any particular branch of trade, however, can never fall in the end on the dealers—who in all ordinary cases must have their reasonable profit, and where competition is free can seldom have more than that profit—but always on the consumers, who are obliged to pay, in the price of the goods, the tax the dealer advances, and generally with something added on top.

A tax of this kind, when it is geared to the dealer's trade, is finally paid by the consumer and causes no hardship to the dealer. When it is not so geared but is the same on all dealers, then—though again it is finally paid by the consumer—it favours the great dealer and causes some hardship to the small one. The tax of five shillings a week on every hackney-coach, and ten shillings a year on every hackney-chair, so far as it is advanced by the various keepers of such coaches and chairs, is geared exactly enough to the extent of their respective dealings. It neither favours the great dealer nor oppresses the smaller. The tax of twenty shillings a year for a licence to sell ale, of forty shillings for a licence to sell spirituous liquors, and of forty shillings more for a licence to sell wine, being the same on all retailers, must necessarily give some advantage to the great dealer and cause some hardship to the small ones. The former finds it easier to recover the tax in the price of his goods than the latter. The moderation of the tax, however, makes this unevenness less important; and many people may think it not improper to give some discouragement to the multiplying of little alehouses. The tax on shops was meant to be the same on all shops. It could hardly have been otherwise. It would have been impossible to gear the tax on a shop, with tolerable exactness, to the extent of the trade carried on in it, without an inquiry that would have been altogether unbearable in a free country. If the tax had been large, it would have oppressed the small dealers and forced almost the whole retail trade into the hands of the great ones. With the competition of the small dealers removed, the great ones would have enjoyed a monopoly of the trade and, like all other monopolists, would soon have combined to raise their profits far beyond what was needed to pay the tax. The final payment, instead of falling on the shopkeeper, would have fallen on the consumer, with a considerable addition to the shopkeeper's profit. For these reasons the plan of a tax on shops was dropped, and the subsidy of 1759 was put in its place.
What is called the personal taille in France is perhaps the most important tax on the profits of stock employed in agriculture levied anywhere in Europe.

In the disordered state of Europe under feudal government, the sovereign had to content himself with taxing those too weak to refuse to pay. The great lords, though willing to help him in particular emergencies, refused to submit to any standing tax, and he was not strong enough to force them. Across Europe the occupiers of land were, for the most part, originally bondmen. Throughout most of Europe they were gradually emancipated. Some acquired ownership of landed estates, which they held by some base or ignoble tenure, sometimes under the king and sometimes under some other great lord, like the old copyholders of England. Others, without acquiring ownership, obtained leases for terms of years on the lands they occupied under their lord, and so became less dependent on him. The great lords seem to have looked on the degree of prosperity and independence this lower order of men had come to enjoy with a spiteful and contemptuous indignation, and willingly agreed that the sovereign should tax them. In some countries this tax was confined to lands held in ownership by an ignoble tenure, and in that case the taille was called real. The land tax set up by the late king of Sardinia, and the taille in the provinces of Languedoc, Provence, Dauphine, and Brittany, in the generality of Montauban, and in the elections of Agen and Condom, as well as in some other districts of France, are taxes on lands held in ownership by an ignoble tenure. In other countries the tax was laid on the supposed profits of all those who held lands belonging to others in farm or lease, whatever the tenure by which the owner held them; and in that case the taille was called personal. In most of those provinces of France called the countries of elections, the taille is of this kind. The real taille, since it is imposed only on part of the country's lands, is necessarily an uneven tax, but not always an arbitrary one, though it is arbitrary on some occasions. The personal taille, since it is meant to be geared to the profits of a certain class of people—profits that can only be guessed at—is necessarily both arbitrary and uneven.

In France the personal taille currently (1775) imposed each year on the twenty generalities called the countries of elections comes to 40,107,239 livres, 16 sous. {Memoires concernant les Droits, etc tom. ii, p.17.} The proportion in which this sum is assessed on those different provinces varies from year to year, according to the reports made to the king's council about the goodness or badness of the crops, as well as other circumstances that may raise or lower their respective abilities to pay. Each generality is divided into a certain number of elections, and the proportion in which the sum laid on the whole generality is split among those elections likewise varies from year to year, according to the reports made to the council about their respective abilities. It seems impossible for the council, even with the best intentions, ever to gear either of these two assessments, with tolerable exactness, to the real abilities of the province or district they are laid on. Ignorance and misinformation must always mislead even the most upright council, more or less. The proportion each parish should bear of what is assessed on the whole election, and the proportion each individual should bear of what is assessed on his particular parish, are both likewise varied from year to year as circumstances are supposed to require. These circumstances are judged in the one case by the officers of the election and in the other by those of the parish, and both are more or less under the direction and influence of the intendant. Not only ignorance and misinformation, but friendship, party animosity, and private resentment are said often to mislead such assessors. Clearly no man subject to such a tax can ever be certain, before he is assessed, of what he will have to pay. He cannot even be certain after he is assessed. If anyone has been taxed who should have been exempt, or taxed beyond his proper share, both must pay in the meantime; but if they complain and make good their complaints, the whole parish is reassessed the next year to repay them. If any of the contributors goes bankrupt or insolvent, the collector must advance his tax, and the whole parish is reassessed the next year to repay the collector. If the collector himself goes bankrupt, the parish that elected him must answer for his conduct to the receiver-general of the election. But since it might be troublesome for the receiver to prosecute the whole parish, he picks five or six of the richest contributors and forces them to make good what was lost through the collector's insolvency. The parish is afterwards reassessed to repay those five or six. Such reassessments are always over and above the taille of the particular year in which they are laid on.

When a tax is laid on the profits of stock in a particular branch of trade, the traders are all careful to bring no more goods to market than they can sell at a price high enough to reimburse them for advancing the tax. Some of them pull part of their stock out of the trade, and the market is supplied more sparingly than before. The price of the goods rises, and the final payment of the tax falls on the consumer. But when a tax is laid on the profits of stock employed in agriculture, it is not in the farmers' interest to pull any part of their stock out of that employment. Each farmer occupies a certain quantity of land for which he pays rent. Properly cultivating this land takes a certain quantity of stock, and by withdrawing any part of that necessary quantity the farmer is not likely to be any better able to pay either the rent or the tax. To pay the tax, it can never be in his interest to reduce the quantity of his produce, and so to supply the market more sparingly than before. The tax will therefore never let him raise the price of his produce so as to reimburse himself by throwing the final payment onto the consumer. The farmer, however, must have his reasonable profit like every other dealer, or he must give up the trade. After a tax of this kind is imposed, he can get this reasonable profit only by paying less rent to the landlord. The more he has to pay in tax, the less he can afford to pay in rent. A tax of this kind, imposed during the term of a lease, may no doubt distress or ruin the farmer. On the renewal of the lease, it must always fall on the landlord.

In countries where the personal taille is in force, the farmer is usually assessed in proportion to the stock he appears to employ in cultivation. For this reason he is often afraid to keep a good team of horses or oxen, and tries instead to cultivate with the meanest and most wretched farming tools he can. So little does he trust in the fairness of his assessors that he fakes poverty and wants to seem barely able to pay anything, for fear of being made to pay too much. By this miserable strategy he probably does not always serve his own interest in the most effective way; he likely loses more through the reduction of his produce than he saves through the reduction of his tax. Though this wretched cultivation no doubt leaves the market somewhat worse supplied, the small rise in price it may cause is not even likely to make up for the farmer's loss of produce, let alone enable him to pay more rent to the landlord. The public, the farmer, and the landlord all suffer more or less from this degraded cultivation. That the personal taille tends in many ways to discourage cultivation, and so to dry up the chief source of the wealth of every great country, I have already had occasion to remark in the third book of this Inquiry.

What are called poll-taxes in the southern provinces of North America and the West India islands—annual taxes of so much a head on every negro—are properly taxes on the profits of a certain kind of stock employed in agriculture. Since the planters are mostly both farmers and landlords, the final payment of the tax falls on them in their capacity as landlords, with no one to pass it on to.

Taxes of so much a head on the bondmen employed in cultivation seem in ancient times to have been common all over Europe. A tax of this kind still exists in the empire of Russia. It is probably on this account that poll-taxes of every sort have often been portrayed as badges of slavery. To the person who pays it, however, every tax is a badge not of slavery but of liberty. It marks him as subject to government, true; but it also marks that, having some property of his own, he cannot himself be the property of a master. A poll-tax on slaves is altogether different from a poll-tax on free men. The latter is paid by the very persons it is imposed on; the former by a different set of people. The latter is either wholly arbitrary or wholly uneven, and in most cases is both; the former, though uneven in some respects, since different slaves are of different values, is in no respect arbitrary. Every master who knows the number of his own slaves knows exactly what he has to pay. These different taxes, however, being called by the same name, have been treated as being of the same nature.

The taxes imposed in Holland on menservants and maidservants are taxes not on stock but on expense, and so resemble taxes on consumable commodities. The tax of a guinea a head for every manservant, lately imposed in Great Britain, is of the same kind. It falls heaviest on the middling rank. A man of two hundred a year may keep a single manservant. A man of ten thousand a year will not keep fifty. It does not affect the poor.

Taxes on the profits of stock in particular employments can never affect the interest of money. Nobody will lend his money at less interest to those in the taxed employments than to those in the untaxed ones. Taxes on the revenue arising from stock in all employments, where the government tries to levy them with any degree of exactness, will in many cases fall on the interest of money. The vingtieme, or twentieth penny, in France is a tax of the same kind as what is called the land tax in England, and is assessed in the same way on the revenue arising from land, houses, and stock. So far as it affects stock, it is assessed—though not with great rigour—yet with much more exactness than the part of the English land tax laid on the same fund. In many cases it falls entirely on the interest of money. In France money is often sunk in what are called contracts for the constitution of a rent—that is, perpetual annuities, redeemable at any time by the debtor on repaying the sum originally advanced, but where this redemption cannot be demanded by the creditor except in particular cases. The vingtieme seems not to have raised the rate of those annuities, though it is levied exactly on them all.
APPENDIX TO ARTICLES I. AND II.—Taxes on the Capital Value of Lands, Houses, and Stock.

While property stays in the hands of the same person, whatever permanent taxes may have been imposed on it have never been meant to reduce or take away any part of its capital value, but only some part of the revenue arising from it. But when property changes hands—when it passes either from the dead to the living, or from the living to the living—taxes have often been imposed on it that necessarily take away some part of its capital value.

When property passes from the dead to the living, and when land or houses pass from one living person to another, the transaction is by its nature either public and well known or impossible to keep hidden for long. Transactions like these can therefore be taxed directly. But when moveable property or capital passes from one living person to another through the lending of money, the transaction is often secret, and it can always be kept secret. So it cannot easily be taxed directly. Instead it has been taxed indirectly in two ways. First, the law has required that the deed recording the obligation to repay be written on paper or parchment that has paid a certain stamp duty; without that stamp the deed is invalid. Second, the law has required, under the same penalty of invalidity, that the deed be recorded in a register, whether public or secret, and has charged duties on that registration. Stamp duties and registration duties have often been imposed in the same way on deeds transferring all kinds of property from the dead to the living, and on those transferring land or houses between living people, even though such transactions could easily have been taxed directly.

The vicesima hereditatum, the twentieth penny on inheritances that Augustus imposed on the ancient Romans, was a tax on the transfer of property from the dead to the living. Dion Cassius (Book 55; see also Burman, de Vectigalibus Pop. Rom., chapter 11, and Bouchaud, de l'impôt du vingtième sur les successions), the author who describes it least obscurely, says it was charged on all inheritances, legacies, and gifts made at death, except for those passing to the closest relatives and to the poor.

The Dutch tax on inheritances is of the same kind (see Mémoires concernant les Droits, etc., volume 1, page 225). Inheritances passing to relatives outside the direct line are taxed by degree of kinship, anywhere from five to thirty per cent of the whole value of the inheritance. Legacies left to such collateral relatives carry the same duties. A bequest from husband to wife, or from wife to husband, pays a fiftieth penny. The luctuosa hereditas, the sorrowful inheritance in which parents inherit from their children, pays only a twentieth penny. Direct inheritances, in which children inherit from their parents, pay no tax at all. When a father dies, the children who lived with him in the same house rarely gain any income from it, and often lose a great deal, since his work, his office, or some life-tenancy he held all come to an end. A tax that worsened that loss by stripping away part of his estate would be cruel and oppressive. The case may sometimes be different, though, for children who, in the language of Roman law, are said to be "emancipated," and in Scots law to be "foris-familiated": that is, children who have already received their share, started families of their own, and are supported by funds separate from and independent of their father's. Whatever part of his estate reached such children would be a genuine addition to their fortune, and might therefore perhaps bear some tax without causing any more hardship than duties of this kind generally do. Under feudal law, the casualties were taxes on the transfer of land, both from the dead to the living and between living people. In earlier times they made up one of the chief sources of the crown's revenue everywhere in Europe.

Whenever an immediate vassal of the crown died, his heir paid a certain duty, usually a year's rent, in order to receive formal possession of the estate. If the heir was a minor, all the rents of the estate went to the lord for the whole of the minority, the lord's only charges being the upkeep of the minor and the payment of the widow's portion, when there happened to be a widow on the land. When the minor came of age, a further tax called relief was still owed to the lord, and it too generally came to a year's rent. A long minority, which today so often clears a great estate of its debts and restores a family to its former splendour, could have no such effect in those days. Back then a long minority commonly wasted the estate rather than freeing it from debt.

Under feudal law a vassal could not sell his land without his lord's consent, and the lord usually extracted a fine or payment for granting it. This fine, at first set arbitrarily, came in many countries to be fixed at a certain share of the land's price. In some countries, where most other feudal customs have died out, this tax on the sale of land still makes up a very large part of the sovereign's revenue. In the canton of Bern it runs as high as a sixth of the price of all noble fiefs and a tenth of the price of all common ones (Mémoires concernant les Droits, etc., volume 1, page 154). In the canton of Lucerne the tax on land sales is not charged everywhere, but only in certain districts. Yet anyone who sells his land in order to move out of the territory pays ten per cent on the whole sale price (id., page 157). Taxes of the same kind, on the sale either of all land or of land held under certain tenures, exist in many other countries and make up a larger or smaller part of the sovereign's revenue.

Transactions like these can be taxed indirectly, either through stamp duties or through registration duties, and those duties may or may not be set in proportion to the value of what is being transferred.

In Great Britain the stamp duties vary more according to the type of deed than according to the value of the property transferred: an eighteen-penny or half-crown stamp is enough on a bond for the largest sum of money. The highest duties do not go above six pounds for each sheet of paper or skin of parchment, and these high duties fall mainly on grants from the crown and on certain legal proceedings, regardless of the value involved. In Great Britain there are no duties on registering deeds or documents, apart from the fees of the officials who keep the register, and these are rarely more than fair pay for their work. The crown gets no revenue from them.

In Holland there are both stamp duties and registration duties (Mémoires concernant les Droits, etc., volume 1, pages 223, 224, 225), and in some cases they are set in proportion to the value of the property transferred while in others they are not. Every will must be written on stamped paper whose price is proportioned to the property being disposed of, so the stamps range from three pence (three stivers) a sheet up to three hundred florins, which equals about twenty-seven pounds ten shillings of our money. If the stamp is of a lower price than the one the testator should have used, his estate is confiscated. This is on top of all their other inheritance taxes. Apart from bills of exchange and certain other commercial bills, every other deed, bond, and contract is subject to a stamp duty, though this duty does not rise in proportion to the value involved. Every sale of land or houses, and every mortgage on either, must be registered, and on registration pays the state a duty of two and a half per cent on the price or the mortgage amount. This duty extends to the sale of all ships and vessels of more than two tons, whether decked or undecked; apparently these count as a kind of house upon the water. The sale of moveable goods, when ordered by a court of justice, is subject to the same two and a half per cent duty.

In France there are both stamp duties and registration duties. The stamp duties are treated as a branch of the excise aids and, in the provinces where they apply, are collected by the excise officers. The registration duties are treated as a branch of the crown's domain and are collected by a different set of officers.

These methods of taxation, through stamp duties and registration duties, are a very recent invention. Yet in little more than a century stamp duties have become almost universal in Europe, and registration duties extremely common. There is no skill that one government learns from another faster than the art of draining money from people's pockets.

Taxes on the transfer of property from the dead to the living fall, in the end as well as immediately, on the people who receive the property. Taxes on the sale of land fall entirely on the seller. The seller is almost always forced to sell and must therefore take whatever price he can get. The buyer is hardly ever forced to buy and will therefore give only the price he chooses. He considers what the land will cost him in tax and price together, so the more he must pay in tax, the less he is willing to give in price. Such taxes therefore almost always fall on someone in need, and so are often very cruel and oppressive. Taxes on the sale of newly built houses, where the building is sold without the ground, generally fall on the buyer, because the builder must have his profit or he will give up the trade; so if he pays the tax up front, the buyer normally repays it to him. Taxes on the sale of old houses, for the same reason as those on land, generally fall on the seller, who in most cases is driven to sell by convenience or necessity. The number of newly built houses brought to market each year is more or less governed by demand: unless demand is high enough to give the builder his profit after all his expenses, he will build no more houses. But the number of old houses that happen to reach the market at any time is governed by accidents, most of which have nothing to do with demand. Two or three big bankruptcies in a trading town will throw many houses onto the market, and they must be sold for whatever they will fetch. Taxes on the sale of ground-rents fall entirely on the seller, for the same reason as those on land. Stamp duties and registration duties on bonds and loan contracts fall entirely on the borrower, and in fact are always paid by him. Duties of the same kind on legal proceedings fall on the parties to the lawsuit. Both kinds reduce the capital value of the property at stake, since the more it costs to acquire a property, the less its net value will be once acquired.

All taxes on the transfer of property of any kind, insofar as they reduce its capital value, tend to shrink the funds that support productive labour. They are all, to some degree, wasteful taxes: they raise the revenue of the sovereign, who rarely supports anyone but unproductive workers, at the expense of the people's capital, which supports only productive ones.

Even when such taxes are set in proportion to the value of the property transferred, they are still unequal, because property of equal value does not always change hands equally often. When they are not proportioned to that value, which is true of most stamp duties and registration duties, they are more unequal still. In no respect are they arbitrary; they are, or can be, perfectly clear and certain in every case. Although they sometimes fall on someone not well able to pay, the moment of payment is in most cases convenient enough for him, since when the tax falls due he will usually have the more to pay it with. They are collected at very little expense and generally subject those who pay them to no inconvenience beyond the unavoidable one of paying. In France the stamp duties are not much complained of, but the registration duties, which the French call the Contrôle, are. They are said to give the officers of the farmers-general who collect them plenty of room for extortion, since the tax is largely arbitrary and uncertain. In most of the pamphlets attacking the present French financial system, the abuses of the Contrôle are a leading complaint. Yet uncertainty does not seem to be a necessary feature of such taxes. If the popular complaints are well founded, the abuse must come not so much from the nature of the tax as from the lack of precision and clarity in the wording of the edicts or laws that impose it.

Registering mortgages, and in general all claims on land and houses, gives great security to both creditors and buyers and is therefore highly beneficial to the public. But registering most other kinds of deeds is often inconvenient and even dangerous to individuals, with no public benefit at all. Any register that is admitted to need keeping secret ought certainly never to exist. A person's credit ought certainly never to rest on something as flimsy as the honesty and conscience of the lower revenue officers. Yet wherever registration fees have been turned into a source of revenue for the sovereign, register-offices have usually multiplied without end, covering both the deeds that ought to be registered and those that ought not. In France there are several different sorts of secret registers. This abuse, though perhaps not strictly necessary, must be admitted to be a very natural result of such taxes.

Stamp duties like those in England on cards and dice, on newspapers and periodical pamphlets, and so on, are really taxes on consumption: the final payment falls on the people who use or consume those goods. Stamp duties like those on licences to sell ale, wine, and spirits, though perhaps meant to fall on the retailers' profits, are likewise paid in the end by the people who drink those liquors. Such taxes, though they go by the same name, are collected by the same officers, and are levied in the same way as the stamp duties already mentioned on the transfer of property, are nonetheless quite different in nature and fall on quite different funds.
ARTICLE III. Taxes on the Wages of Labour.

In the first book I tried to show that the wages of the lower classes of workers are everywhere necessarily governed by two things: the demand for labour and the ordinary or average price of food and other provisions. Whether the demand for labour is rising, steady, or falling, and whether it calls for a growing, steady, or shrinking population, determines how the labourer is provided for and whether his subsistence is generous, modest, or meagre. The ordinary average price of provisions then determines how much money he must be paid to buy that generous, modest, or meagre subsistence, year in and year out. So long as the demand for labour and the price of provisions stay the same, a direct tax on wages can do nothing but push wages somewhat higher than the tax itself. Suppose, for example, that in some place the demand for labour and the price of provisions made ten shillings a week the ordinary wage, and that a tax of one-fifth, or four shillings in the pound, was laid on wages. If the demand for labour and the price of provisions stayed the same, the labourer would still need to earn enough to buy a subsistence that cost ten shillings a week, so that after paying the tax he would have ten shillings a week left as free wages. But to leave him those free wages after such a tax, the price of labour in that place must soon rise not just to twelve shillings a week but to twelve shillings and sixpence: that is, to let him pay a tax of one-fifth, his wages must soon rise not by a fifth but by a quarter. Whatever the proportion of the tax, wages must in every case rise not merely in that proportion but in a higher one. If the tax were a tenth, for instance, wages must soon rise not by a tenth but by an eighth.

A direct tax on wages, then, even if the labourer paid it out of his own hand, could not properly be said to be even fronted by him, at least if the demand for labour and the average price of provisions stayed the same after the tax as before. In every such case, not just the tax but something more than the tax would really be fronted by whoever directly employed him. The final payment would fall, in different cases, on different people. The rise in manufacturing wages caused by such a tax would be fronted by the master manufacturer, who would be both entitled and obliged to add it, with a profit, to the price of his goods; so the final payment of the wage rise, together with the manufacturer's extra profit, would fall on the consumer. The rise in farm wages caused by such a tax would be fronted by the farmer, who, to keep the same number of labourers as before, would have to put up more capital. To recover this larger capital along with the ordinary profit on it, he would have to keep a larger share, or what comes to the same thing the price of a larger share, of the land's produce, and so would pay less rent to the landlord. In this case, then, the final payment of the wage rise would fall on the landlord, together with the extra profit of the farmer who fronted it. In every case, a direct tax on wages must in the long run cause both a greater fall in the rent of land and a greater rise in the price of manufactured goods than would have followed from properly assessing a sum equal to the tax's yield, partly on the rent of land and partly on consumable goods.

If direct taxes on wages have not always produced a matching rise in wages, it is because they have generally caused a sharp drop in the demand for labour. The decline of industry, the loss of work for the poor, and the shrinking of the country's yearly produce of land and labour have generally been the effects of such taxes. As a result, the price of labour must always be higher than it otherwise would be given the actual level of demand, and this added cost, together with the profit of those who front it, must always be paid in the end by landlords and consumers.

A tax on the wages of farm labour does not raise the price of the raw produce of the land in proportion to the tax, for the same reason that a tax on the farmer's profit does not raise that price in proportion.

Absurd and destructive as such taxes are, they nonetheless exist in many countries. In France the part of the taille charged on the work of artisans and day-labourers in country villages is really a tax of this kind. Their wages are reckoned by the ordinary rate of the district where they live, and, so that they may be as little overcharged as possible, their yearly earnings are figured at no more than two hundred working days in the year (Mémoires concernant les Droits, etc., volume 2, page 108). Each person's tax varies from year to year according to circumstances judged by the collector, or by the commissary the intendant appoints to assist him. In Bohemia, following the change to the financial system begun in 1748, a very heavy tax is laid on the work of craftsmen. They are divided into four classes. The highest class pays a hundred florins a year, which at twenty-two and a half pence to the florin comes to £9 7s 6d. The second class is taxed at seventy florins, the third at fifty, and the fourth, which takes in village craftsmen and the lowest class of those in towns, at twenty-five florins (Mémoires concernant les Droits, etc., volume 3, page 87).

In the first book I tried to show that the earnings of skilled artists and of men in the learned professions necessarily keep a certain proportion to the earnings of lower trades. A tax on these earnings, therefore, could do nothing but raise them somewhat more than in proportion to the tax. If they did not rise in this way, the skilled arts and learned professions, no longer on a level with other trades, would be so widely abandoned that they would soon return to that level.

The earnings of public offices are not, like those of trades and professions, set by free competition in the market, and so they do not always bear a fair proportion to what the work itself requires. In most countries they are probably higher than it requires, since those who run the government are generally inclined to look after themselves and their close dependents rather more than they should. The earnings of offices, then, can in most cases well afford to be taxed. Besides, those who hold public offices, especially the more profitable ones, are objects of general envy in every country, so a tax on their earnings, even one a bit higher than on any other kind of income, is always very popular. In England, for example, when the land tax was supposed to assess every other kind of income at four shillings in the pound, it was very popular to lay a real tax of five shillings and sixpence in the pound on official salaries above a hundred pounds a year, exempting the pensions of the junior royals, the pay of army and navy officers, and a few others less open to envy. There are no other direct taxes on wages in England.
ARTICLE IV. Taxes meant to fall without distinction on every different kind of revenue.

The taxes meant to fall without distinction on every kind of revenue are capitation taxes and taxes on consumable goods. These must be paid no matter what kind of income the contributors have, whether it comes from the rent of their land, the profits of their capital, or the wages of their labour.
Capitation Taxes.

If you try to proportion capitation taxes to each contributor's fortune or income, they become completely arbitrary. A man's fortune changes from day to day, and without an inquisition more unbearable than any tax, repeated at least once a year, it can only be guessed at. His assessment, then, must in most cases depend on the good or bad mood of his assessors, and so must be wholly arbitrary and uncertain.
If capitation taxes are proportioned not to a man's supposed fortune but to his rank, they become completely unequal, since fortunes often differ widely among people of the same rank.

Such taxes, then, become wholly arbitrary and uncertain if you try to make them equal, and wholly unequal if you try to make them certain and not arbitrary. Whether the tax is light or heavy, uncertainty is always a great grievance. With a light tax a fair degree of inequality can be endured; with a heavy one it is altogether unbearable.

In the various poll taxes levied in England during the reign of William III, most contributors were assessed according to their rank: as dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, barons, esquires, gentlemen, the eldest and youngest sons of peers, and so on. All shopkeepers and tradesmen worth more than three hundred pounds, meaning the better-off among them, were charged the same amount, however much their fortunes might differ. Rank counted for more than fortune. Several people who in the first poll tax had been rated by their supposed fortune were later rated by their rank. Sergeants, attorneys, and proctors at law, who in the first poll tax had been charged three shillings in the pound on their supposed income, were afterwards charged simply as gentlemen. In assessing a tax that was not very heavy, a fair degree of inequality had proved less intolerable than any degree of uncertainty.

In the capitation levied in France without interruption since the start of the present century, the highest ranks are rated by their rank, under a fixed schedule, while the lower ranks are rated by their supposed fortune, under an assessment that changes from year to year. The officers of the king's court, the judges and other officers of the higher courts of justice, the officers of the army, and so on, are assessed in the first way. The lower ranks in the provinces are assessed in the second. In France the great readily put up with a fair degree of inequality in a tax that, as it affects them, is not very heavy, but they could not stomach the arbitrary assessment of an intendant.
The lower ranks in that country must patiently bear whatever treatment their superiors see fit to give them.

In England the various poll taxes never raised the sum that had been expected of them, or that they were thought capable of raising if collected exactly. In France the capitation always raises the sum expected. The mild government of England, when it assessed the different ranks for the poll tax, was content with whatever the assessment happened to bring in, and asked no compensation for what the state might lose through those who could not pay, or those who would not pay, of whom there were many, and who under the lenient enforcement of the law were not forced to pay. The harsher government of France assesses each généralité at a fixed sum, which the intendant must somehow raise. If a province complains of being assessed too high, it may get a reduction in the next year's assessment to match the overcharge of the year before, but in the meantime it must pay. To make sure of raising the sum assessed on his généralité, the intendant was authorised to assess a larger amount, so that the failure or inability of some contributors could be made up by overcharging the rest, and until 1765 the size of this surplus assessment was left entirely to his discretion. In that year, however, the council took this power to itself. As the perfectly well-informed author of the Memoirs on the Impositions in France observes, in the capitation of the provinces the share falling on the nobility, and on those whose privileges exempt them from the taille, is the smallest. The largest share falls on those subject to the taille, who are assessed to the capitation at so much per pound of what they pay to that other tax. Capitation taxes, so far as they are levied on the lower ranks, are direct taxes on wages and carry all the same drawbacks as such taxes.

Capitation taxes are collected at little expense and, where they are strictly enforced, give the state a very reliable revenue. That is why they are so common in countries where the ease, comfort, and security of the lower ranks count for little. Still, in a great empire only a small part of the public revenue has ever been drawn from such taxes, and the largest sum they have ever yielded could always have been raised some other way far more convenient to the people.
Taxes on Consumable Goods.

The impossibility of taxing people in proportion to their income through any capitation seems to be what prompted the invention of taxes on consumable goods. Not knowing how to tax its subjects' income directly and proportionably, the state tries to tax it indirectly by taxing their spending, which is assumed to be roughly proportional to their income in most cases. Their spending is taxed by taxing the consumable goods they spend it on.
Consumable goods are either necessities or luxuries.

By necessities I mean not only the things absolutely required to keep alive, but whatever the custom of the country makes it unseemly for respectable people, even of the lowest rank, to go without. A linen shirt, for instance, is strictly speaking not a necessity of life. The Greeks and Romans lived quite comfortably, I suppose, though they had no linen. But in our times, through most of Europe, a respectable day-labourer would be ashamed to appear in public without a linen shirt, whose absence would be taken to mark that disgraceful poverty which, it is assumed, no one falls into without grave misconduct. In the same way custom has made leather shoes a necessity of life in England. The poorest respectable person, man or woman, would be ashamed to appear in public without them. In Scotland custom has made them a necessity for the lowest rank of men, but not for women of the same rank, who may walk about barefoot with no loss of respect. In France they are necessities for neither men nor women; there the lowest rank of both sexes appears in public without disgrace, sometimes in wooden shoes and sometimes barefoot. Under necessities, then, I include not only the things nature has made necessary but the things the established rules of decency have made necessary for the lowest rank. Everything else I call a luxury, without meaning by that word to cast the slightest reproach on the moderate use of such things. Beer and ale in Great Britain, for example, and wine even in the wine-producing countries, I call luxuries. A man of any rank may abstain entirely from such drinks without any reproach. Nature does not make them necessary for survival, and nowhere does custom make it improper to live without them.

Since wages everywhere are set partly by the demand for labour and partly by the average price of the necessary articles of subsistence, whatever raises that average price must necessarily raise wages, so that the labourer can still buy the quantity of necessities that the state of labour demand, whether rising, steady, or falling, requires him to have (see Book I, chapter 8). A tax on those articles necessarily raises their price somewhat above the amount of the tax, because the dealer who fronts the tax must normally recover it with a profit. Such a tax must therefore cause wages to rise in proportion to this rise in price.

So a tax on the necessities of life works in exactly the same way as a direct tax on wages. The labourer, though he may pay it out of his own hand, cannot, at least for any length of time, properly be said even to front it. In the long run it must always be fronted to him by his immediate employer through higher wages. If that employer is a manufacturer, he will add the wage rise, together with a profit, to the price of his goods, so that the final payment of the tax, together with this added charge, falls on the consumer. If the employer is a farmer, the final payment, together with a similar added charge, falls on the landlord's rent.

It is different with taxes on what I call luxuries, even the luxuries of the poor. The rise in the price of the taxed goods will not necessarily cause any rise in wages. A tax on tobacco, for instance, though a luxury of the poor as well as the rich, will not raise wages. Even though tobacco is taxed in England at three times, and in France at fifteen times, its original price, those high duties seem to have no effect on wages. The same can be said of the taxes on tea and sugar, which in England and Holland have become luxuries of even the lowest ranks, and of those on chocolate, which in Spain is said to have become one too.

The various taxes that have been laid on spirits in Great Britain over the course of the present century are not thought to have had any effect on wages. The rise in the price of porter caused by an extra tax of three shillings on the barrel of strong beer has not raised the wages of common labour in London. These were about eighteen or twenty pence a day before the tax, and they are no higher now.

The high price of such goods does not necessarily reduce the ability of the lower ranks to raise families. On the sober and hardworking poor, taxes on such goods act like sumptuary laws, prompting them either to cut down on, or to give up entirely, luxuries they can no longer easily afford. Their ability to raise families, far from being reduced by this forced thrift, is perhaps often increased by the tax. It is the sober and hardworking poor who generally raise the largest families and who chiefly supply the demand for useful labour. Not all the poor, of course, are sober and hardworking, and the dissolute and disorderly might go on indulging in such goods after the price rises, just as before, heedless of the hardship this indulgence brings on their families. But such disorderly people rarely raise large families: their children generally die of neglect, mismanagement, and food that is too scarce or unwholesome. And if by their strong constitutions the children survive the hardships their parents' bad conduct exposes them to, the example of that bad conduct commonly corrupts their morals, so that instead of being useful to society by their work they become public nuisances by their vices and disorders. So although the higher price of the luxuries of the poor might somewhat worsen the distress of such disorderly families, and thereby somewhat lessen their ability to raise children, it would probably not greatly reduce the country's useful population.

Any rise in the average price of necessities, unless matched by a proportionate rise in wages, must necessarily reduce, more or less, the ability of the poor to raise large families and so to supply the demand for useful labour, whatever the state of that demand, whether rising, steady, or falling, and whether it calls for a growing, steady, or shrinking population.

Taxes on luxuries have no tendency to raise the price of anything but the taxed goods themselves. Taxes on necessities, by raising wages, necessarily tend to raise the price of all manufactures, and so to shrink the extent of their sale and consumption. Taxes on luxuries are paid in the end by the consumers of the taxed goods, with no recompense. They fall without distinction on every kind of revenue: wages, the profits of capital, and the rent of land. Taxes on necessities, so far as they affect the labouring poor, are paid in the end partly by landlords, through the reduced rent of their land, and partly by rich consumers, whether landlords or not, through the higher price of manufactured goods, and always with a considerable added charge. The higher price of those manufactures that are real necessities of life, made for the poor to consume, such as coarse woollens, must be made up to the poor by a further rise in their wages. The middling and upper ranks, if they understood their own interest, ought always to oppose all taxes on the necessities of life, as well as all taxes on wages. The final payment of both falls entirely on themselves, and always with a considerable added charge. It falls heaviest on the landlords, who always pay twice over: as landlords, through reduced rent, and as rich consumers, through increased spending. Sir Matthew Decker's observation that certain taxes are sometimes repeated and piled up four or five times in the price of certain goods is perfectly true of taxes on the necessities of life. In the price of leather, for example, you pay not only the tax on the leather of your own shoes but part of the tax on those of the shoemaker and the tanner. You also pay the tax on the salt, soap, and candles those workmen use while working for you, and the tax on the leather that the saltmaker, the soap-maker, and the candle-maker use while working at their own trades.
In Great Britain the chief taxes on the necessities of life are those on the four goods just mentioned: salt, leather, soap, and candles.

Salt is a very ancient and very widespread subject of taxation. It was taxed among the Romans, and it is taxed today in, I believe, every part of Europe. The amount each person consumes in a year is so small, and can be bought so gradually, that nobody, it seems to have been thought, could feel even a fairly heavy tax on it very keenly. In England it is taxed at three shillings and fourpence a bushel, about three times the original price of the goods. In some other countries the tax is higher still. Leather is a real necessity of life. The use of linen makes soap one too. In countries where the winter nights are long, candles are a necessary tool of trade. Leather and soap are taxed in Great Britain at three halfpence a pound, candles at a penny: taxes that come to about eight or ten per cent on the original price of leather, about twenty or twenty-five per cent on that of soap, and about fourteen or fifteen per cent on that of candles. These taxes, though lighter than the one on salt, are still very heavy. Since all four of these goods are real necessities of life, such heavy taxes on them must add somewhat to the expenses of the sober and hardworking poor, and so must raise their wages more or less.

In a country with winters as cold as Britain's, fuel during that season is, in the strictest sense, a necessity of life, not only for cooking food but for the comfortable subsistence of many kinds of workmen who work indoors; and coal is the cheapest of all fuels. The price of fuel has such an important effect on the price of labour that all over Great Britain manufactures have mostly settled in the coal counties, the rest of the country being unable to produce as cheaply because this necessary article costs so much there. In some manufactures, moreover, coal is a necessary tool of trade, as in those of glass, iron, and all the other metals. If a bounty could ever be reasonable, it might perhaps be so on carrying coal from the parts of the country where it abounds to those where it is wanted. But instead of a bounty the legislature has laid a tax of three shillings and threepence a ton on coal carried by sea, which on most sorts of coal is more than sixty per cent of the original price at the pit. Coal carried by land or by inland waterway pays no duty. Where coal is naturally cheap, it is consumed duty-free; where it is naturally dear, it is loaded with a heavy duty.

Such taxes, though they raise the price of subsistence and therefore wages, do bring the government a considerable revenue that might not easily be found in any other way. There may, then, be good reasons for keeping them. The bounty on exporting corn, so far as it tends, given the actual state of farming, to raise the price of that necessary article, produces all the same bad effects; and instead of bringing in any revenue, it frequently costs the government a great deal. The high duties on importing foreign corn, which in years of moderate plenty amount to a prohibition, and the outright ban on importing live cattle or salt provisions, which holds under the ordinary state of the law and which, because of scarcity, is at present suspended for a limited time for Ireland and the British plantations, have all had the bad effects of taxes on the necessities of life, and bring the government no revenue. To repeal such regulations, nothing seems needed but to convince the public of the worthlessness of the system that gave rise to them.

Taxes on the necessities of life are much higher in many other countries than in Great Britain. Duties on flour and meal when ground at the mill, and on bread when baked at the oven, exist in many countries. In Holland the money price of the bread consumed in the towns is thought to be doubled by such taxes. In place of part of them, country people pay so much a head each year, according to the kind of bread they are supposed to eat. Those who eat wheaten bread pay three guilders fifteen stivers, about six shillings and ninepence halfpenny. These and some other taxes of the same kind, by raising the price of labour, are said to have ruined most of the manufactures of Holland (Mémoires concernant les Droits, etc., pages 210, 211). Similar taxes, though not quite so heavy, exist in the Milanese, in the states of Genoa, in the duchy of Modena, in the duchies of Parma, Piacenza, and Guastalla, and in the Ecclesiastical State. A French writer of some note (Le Réformateur) has proposed to reform his country's finances by replacing most of the other taxes with this most ruinous tax of all. There is nothing so absurd, says Cicero, that some philosopher has not at some time asserted it.

Taxes on butcher's meat are even more common than those on bread. It may indeed be doubted whether butcher's meat is anywhere a necessity of life. Experience shows that grain and other vegetables, with the help of milk, cheese, and butter, or oil where butter is unavailable, can provide without any butcher's meat the most plentiful, wholesome, nourishing, and invigorating diet. Decency nowhere requires a man to eat butcher's meat, as it requires him in most places to wear a linen shirt or a pair of leather shoes.

Consumable goods, whether necessities or luxuries, can be taxed in two ways. The consumer may pay an annual sum for using or consuming goods of a certain kind; or the goods may be taxed while still in the dealer's hands, before they are delivered to the consumer. Goods that last a long time before being completely consumed are most fittingly taxed the first way; those consumed immediately or quickly, the second. The coach tax and the plate tax are examples of the first method; most other excise and customs duties, of the second.

A coach, with good care, may last ten or twelve years. It could be taxed once and for all before it leaves the coach-maker's hands. But it is certainly more convenient for the buyer to pay four pounds a year for the privilege of keeping a coach than to pay all at once forty or forty-eight pounds extra to the coach-maker, a sum equal to what the tax is likely to cost him over the time he uses the same coach. Likewise a service of plate may last more than a century. It is certainly easier for the consumer to pay five shillings a year for every hundred ounces of plate, nearly one per cent of the value, than to buy off this long annuity at twenty-five or thirty years' purchase, which would raise the price by at least twenty-five or thirty per cent. The various taxes that fall on houses are certainly more conveniently paid by moderate annual payments than by one heavy tax of equal value on the first building or sale of the house.

It was Sir Matthew Decker's well-known proposal that all goods, even those consumed immediately or quickly, should be taxed in this way, with the dealer fronting nothing and the consumer paying a fixed annual sum for the licence to consume certain goods. The aim of his scheme was to promote every branch of foreign trade, especially the carrying trade, by removing all import and export duties, so that the merchant could put his whole capital and credit into buying goods and freighting ships, with none of it tied up in fronting taxes. But the plan of taxing goods of immediate or quick consumption in this way seems open to the following four very important objections. First, the tax would be more unequal, less well matched to the spending and consumption of different contributors, than under the usual method. The taxes on ale, wine, and spirits, fronted by the dealers, are paid in the end by the various consumers exactly in proportion to how much each consumes. But if the tax were paid by buying a licence to drink those liquors, the sober man would, relative to what he drinks, be taxed far more heavily than the drunkard. A family that entertained generously would be taxed far more lightly than one that received fewer guests. Second, this method, paying for an annual, half-yearly, or quarterly licence to consume certain goods, would largely destroy one of the chief conveniences of taxes on goods of quick consumption: payment piecemeal. In the threepence-halfpenny now paid for a pot of porter, the various taxes on malt, hops, and beer, together with the extra profit the brewer charges for fronting them, may come to about three halfpence. If a workman can conveniently spare those three halfpence, he buys a pot of porter; if he cannot, he makes do with a pint, and, since a penny saved is a penny earned, he gains a farthing by his moderation. He pays the tax piecemeal, as he can afford it and when he can afford it, and every act of payment is entirely voluntary and can be avoided if he chooses. Third, such taxes would work less effectively as sumptuary laws. Once the licence was bought, whether the buyer drank much or little, his tax would be the same. Fourth, if a workman had to pay all at once, by yearly, half-yearly, or quarterly payments, a tax equal to what he now pays with little or no inconvenience on all the separate pots and pints of porter he drinks over such a period, the sum would often distress him badly. So this method of taxation, it seems clear, could never produce a revenue anywhere near what is got from the present method without the most grievous oppression, while the present method causes no oppression at all. In several countries, however, goods of immediate or very quick consumption are taxed this way. In Holland people pay so much a head for a licence to drink tea. I have already mentioned a tax on bread which, so far as it is consumed in farmhouses and country villages, is levied there in the same manner.

The excise duties are laid chiefly on home-produced goods meant for home consumption. They are laid on only a few sorts of goods in the most general use. There can never be any doubt about which goods are subject to these duties, or about the particular duty each sort of goods bears. They fall almost entirely on what I call luxuries, always excepting the four duties already mentioned on salt, soap, leather, and candles, and perhaps the one on green glass.

The customs duties are much older than the excise duties. They seem to have been called customs because they were customary payments in use from time immemorial. They appear to have been originally regarded as taxes on merchants' profits. In the barbarous times of feudal anarchy, merchants, like all the other inhabitants of the towns, were regarded as little better than freed serfs, their persons despised and their gains envied. The great nobles, who had agreed that the king might tax the profits of their own tenants, were not unwilling that he should also tax the profits of an order of men they had far less interest in protecting. In those ignorant times it was not understood that merchants' profits cannot be taxed directly, or that the final payment of all such taxes must fall, with a considerable added charge, on the consumers.

The gains of foreign merchants were viewed less favourably than those of English merchants. It was natural, then, that the former should be taxed more heavily than the latter. This distinction between the duties on foreigners and those on English merchants, which began from ignorance, has been kept up out of the spirit of monopoly, to give our own merchants an advantage in both the home and the foreign market.

With this distinction, the old customs duties were laid equally on all sorts of goods, necessities as well as luxuries, goods exported as well as goods imported. Why, it seems to have been thought, should dealers in one sort of goods be favoured over dealers in another? Or why should the merchant who exports be favoured over the merchant who imports?

The old customs were divided into three branches. The first, and perhaps the oldest of all these duties, was on wool and leather. It seems to have been chiefly or wholly an export duty. When the woollen manufacture became established in England, a like duty was laid on woollen cloths, so that the king should not lose any of his customs on wool through the export of cloth. The other two branches were, first, a duty on wine, which, being charged at so much a ton, was called a tonnage; and second, a duty on all other goods, which, being charged at so much per pound of their supposed value, was called a poundage. In the forty-seventh year of Edward III a duty of sixpence in the pound was laid on all goods exported and imported, except wool, woolfells, leather, and wine, which were subject to special duties. In the fourteenth year of Richard II this duty was raised to a shilling in the pound, but three years later it was reduced again to sixpence. It was raised to eightpence in the second year of Henry IV, and in the fourth year of the same king to a shilling. From then until the ninth year of William III this duty stayed at a shilling in the pound. The duties of tonnage and poundage were generally granted to the king by one and the same act of parliament, and were called the subsidy of tonnage and poundage. Because the subsidy of poundage stayed so long at a shilling in the pound, or five per cent, the word "subsidy" came in customs language to mean a general duty of this kind of five per cent. This subsidy, now called the old subsidy, is still levied according to the book of rates set by the twelfth year of Charles II. The method of fixing, by a book of rates, the value of goods subject to this duty is said to be older than the time of James I. The new subsidy, imposed in the ninth and tenth years of William III, was an additional five per cent on most goods. The one-third and two-third subsidies together made up another five per cent, of which they were proportionate parts. The subsidy of 1747 made a fourth five per cent on most goods, and that of 1759 a fifth on certain particular sorts of goods. Besides these five subsidies, a great variety of other duties have from time to time been laid on particular sorts of goods, sometimes to meet the state's emergencies and sometimes to regulate the country's trade according to the principles of the mercantile system.

That system has gradually come more and more into fashion. The old subsidy was imposed on exports just as much as on imports. The four later subsidies, along with the other duties since imposed from time to time on particular kinds of goods, have, with a few exceptions, fallen entirely on imports. Most of the ancient duties once levied on the export of home-produced and home-manufactured goods have either been reduced or scrapped altogether; in most cases they have been scrapped. Bounties have even been paid on the export of some of them. Drawbacks too—sometimes the whole and in most cases part of the duties paid on imported foreign goods—have been granted when those goods are re-exported. Only half the duties laid by the old subsidy on imports are refunded on export, but the whole of those laid by the later subsidies and other charges are refunded in the same way on most goods. This growing favour towards exports and discouragement of imports has admitted only a few exceptions, which mainly concern the raw materials of certain manufactures. Our merchants and manufacturers want these materials to reach themselves as cheaply as possible and their rivals and competitors in other countries as dearly as possible. For this reason foreign materials are sometimes allowed in duty-free—Spanish wool, for example, flax, and raw linen yarn. The export of home-produced raw materials, and of those that are the special produce of our colonies, has sometimes been prohibited and sometimes charged higher duties. The export of English wool has been prohibited. That of beaver skins, beaver wool, and gum-senega has been charged higher duties, since Great Britain, by conquering Canada and Senegal, has gained almost a monopoly of those commodities.

I have tried to show, in the fourth book of this Inquiry, that the mercantile system has not been very favourable to the income of the great body of the people, or to the annual produce of the land and labour of the country. It seems to have been no more favourable to the income of the sovereign, at least so far as that income depends on customs duties.

As a result of that system, the import of several kinds of goods has been prohibited altogether. In some cases this prohibition has entirely prevented the import of those commodities, and in others has greatly reduced it, by forcing importers to smuggle. It has entirely prevented the import of foreign woollens, and has greatly reduced that of foreign silks and velvets. In both cases it has completely wiped out the customs revenue that might have been collected on such imports.

The high duties imposed on the import of many different kinds of foreign goods, meant to discourage their consumption in Great Britain, have in many cases done nothing but encourage smuggling, and in all cases have brought in less customs revenue than more moderate duties would have yielded. Dr Swift's remark—that in the arithmetic of the customs, two and two sometimes make only one instead of four—holds perfectly true of such heavy duties, which could never have been imposed had the mercantile system not taught us, in many cases, to use taxation as a tool not of revenue but of monopoly.

The bounties sometimes paid on the export of home produce and manufactures, and the drawbacks paid on the re-export of most foreign goods, have given rise to many frauds and to a kind of smuggling more destructive of the public revenue than any other. To collect the bounty or drawback, the goods are—as is well known—sometimes shipped and sent to sea, then soon afterwards secretly landed again in some other part of the country. The loss of customs revenue caused by bounties and drawbacks, a large part of which are obtained by fraud, is very great. The gross customs revenue in the year that ended on 5 January 1755 came to £5,068,000. The bounties paid out of this revenue, even though there was no corn bounty that year, came to £167,806. The drawbacks paid on debentures and certificates came to £2,156,800. Bounties and drawbacks together came to £2,324,600. After these deductions the customs revenue amounted to only £2,743,400; and after deducting £287,900 for the cost of management—salaries and other incidentals—the net customs revenue for that year works out at £2,455,500. The cost of management thus amounts to between five and six per cent of the gross customs revenue, and to something more than ten per cent of what is left after deducting what is paid out in bounties and drawbacks.

Since heavy duties are imposed on almost everything imported, our importing merchants smuggle as much as they can and declare as little as they can. Our exporting merchants, on the other hand, declare more than they actually export—sometimes out of vanity, to pass as great dealers in goods that pay no duty, and sometimes to claim a bounty on goods that paid duty on import and now earn the duty back. Because of these various frauds, our exports appear in the custom-house books to outweigh our imports by a wide margin, to the boundless satisfaction of those politicians who measure the nation's prosperity by what they call the balance of trade.

All imported goods, unless specifically exempted—and such exemptions are not very numerous—are subject to some customs duties. If goods are imported that are not listed in the book of rates, they are taxed at 4s 9¾ d for every twenty shillings of value, according to the importer's sworn declaration—that is, at nearly five subsidies, or five poundage duties. The book of rates is extremely comprehensive and lists a great variety of articles, many of them little used and therefore not well known. For this reason it is often unclear under which heading a particular kind of goods should be classed, and consequently what duty it should pay. Mistakes about this sometimes ruin the customs officer and often cause the importer much trouble, expense, and aggravation. In clarity, precision, and distinctness, therefore, the customs duties are much inferior to the excise duties.

For most members of a society to contribute to the public revenue in proportion to their respective spending, it does not seem necessary to tax every single item of that spending. The revenue raised by excise duties is supposed to fall as evenly on the contributors as that raised by customs duties, and the excise duties are imposed on only a few articles of the most general use and consumption. Many people have held the view that, with proper management, the customs duties could likewise—without any loss to the public revenue and to the great benefit of foreign trade—be confined to only a few articles.

The foreign articles of most general use and consumption in Great Britain seem at present to consist chiefly of foreign wines and brandies; of some products of America and the West Indies—sugar, rum, tobacco, coconuts, and so on; and of some products of the East Indies—tea, coffee, china-ware, spices of all kinds, several sorts of piece-goods, and so on. These various articles probably yield most of the revenue now drawn from customs duties. The taxes that now exist on foreign manufactures—apart from those on the few articles just listed—have, for the most part, been imposed not for revenue but for monopoly, or to give our own merchants an advantage in the home market. By removing all prohibitions and by subjecting all foreign manufactures to such moderate taxes as experience showed yielded the greatest revenue to the public on each article, our own workers could still keep a considerable advantage in the home market; and many articles, some of which now yield no revenue to the government and others a very small one, might yield a very large one.
High taxes—sometimes by cutting the consumption of the taxed commodities, and sometimes by encouraging smuggling—frequently yield the government less revenue than more moderate taxes would.

When the loss of revenue results from reduced consumption, there is only one remedy: lowering the tax. When the loss of revenue results from the encouragement given to smuggling, it can perhaps be remedied in two ways: either by reducing the temptation to smuggle, or by making smuggling more difficult. The temptation to smuggle can be reduced only by lowering the tax; and the difficulty of smuggling can be increased only by setting up the system of administration best suited to preventing it.

Experience shows, I believe, that the excise laws obstruct and hamper the smuggler far more effectively than the customs laws do. By bringing into the customs a system of administration as much like the excise as the different nature of the duties will allow, the difficulty of smuggling could be greatly increased. Many people have supposed that this change could be brought about quite easily.

It has been suggested that the importer of goods subject to any customs duties might, at his choice, be allowed either to take them to his own private warehouse or to lodge them in a warehouse—provided at his own expense or at the public's—but kept under the lock of the customs officer and never opened except in his presence. If the merchant took them to his own private warehouse, the duties would be paid at once and never afterwards refunded, and that warehouse would be subject at all times to inspection and examination by the customs officer, to check how far the quantity it held matched that on which the duty had been paid. If he took them to the public warehouse, no duty would be paid until they were withdrawn for home consumption. If withdrawn for export, they would be duty-free, proper security always being given that they would indeed be exported. The dealers in those particular commodities, whether wholesale or retail, would be subject at all times to inspection and examination by the customs officer, and would be required to prove, by proper certificates, that duty had been paid on the whole quantity held in their shops or warehouses. The so-called excise duties on imported rum are at present collected in this way, and the same system of administration might perhaps be extended to all duties on imported goods—always provided that those duties were, like the excise duties, confined to a few kinds of goods of the most general use and consumption. If they were extended to almost all kinds of goods, as at present, public warehouses of sufficient size could not easily be provided; and goods of a very delicate nature, or whose preservation required much care and attention, could not safely be entrusted by the merchant to any warehouse but his own.

If such a system of administration could prevent smuggling to any considerable extent, even under fairly high duties; and if every duty were occasionally raised or lowered depending on which way was most likely to yield the greatest revenue to the state—taxation always being used as a tool of revenue and never of monopoly—then it seems quite possible that a revenue at least equal to the present net customs revenue could be drawn from duties on the import of only a few kinds of goods of the most general use and consumption; and the customs duties could thus be brought to the same degree of simplicity, certainty, and precision as the excise duties. What the revenue now loses through drawbacks on the re-export of foreign goods that are afterwards landed again and consumed at home would, under this system, be saved entirely. If to this saving—which alone would be very considerable—one added the abolition of all bounties on the export of home produce (in every case where those bounties were not really drawbacks of excise duties previously advanced), there can be little doubt that, after a change of this kind, the net customs revenue could be fully equal to what it had ever been before.

If, under such a change of system, the public revenue suffered no loss, the trade and manufactures of the country would certainly gain a very considerable advantage. Trade in the untaxed commodities—by far the greatest number—would be perfectly free, and could be carried on to and from all parts of the world with every possible advantage. Among those commodities would be all the necessaries of life and all the raw materials of manufacture. To the extent that the free import of necessaries lowered their average money price in the home market, it would lower the money price of labour, but without lowering its real reward in any way. The value of money is in proportion to the quantity of necessaries it will buy; the value of the necessaries themselves is entirely independent of how much money can be had for them. The fall in the money price of labour would necessarily bring a proportionate fall in the price of all home manufactures, which would thereby gain some advantage in every foreign market. The price of some manufactures would fall even more, through the free import of the raw materials. If raw silk could be imported duty-free from China and Hindustan, the silk manufacturers of England could greatly undersell those of both France and Italy. There would be no need to prohibit the import of foreign silks and velvets. The cheapness of their goods would secure to our own workers not only command of the home market but a great command of the foreign market too. Even trade in the taxed commodities would be carried on much more advantageously than at present. If those commodities were released from the public warehouse for export, being in that case exempt from all taxes, trade in them would be perfectly free. The carrying trade in all kinds of goods would, under this system, enjoy every possible advantage. If those commodities were released for home consumption, the importer—not obliged to advance the tax until he had a chance to sell the goods, either to a dealer or to a consumer—could always afford to sell them more cheaply than if he had been forced to advance the tax at the moment of import. Under the same taxes, the foreign trade in consumer goods, even in the taxed commodities, could in this way be carried on much more advantageously than it now is.

The famous excise scheme of Sir Robert Walpole aimed to set up, for wine and tobacco, a system not very unlike the one proposed here. But although the bill then brought into Parliament covered only those two commodities, it was generally supposed to be meant as the opening of a more extensive scheme of the same kind. Faction, joined with the interest of smuggling merchants, raised so violent—though so unjust—an outcry against that bill that the minister thought it best to drop it; and, fearing a similar outcry, none of his successors have dared to revive the project.

The duties on foreign luxuries imported for home consumption, though they sometimes fall on the poor, fall mainly on people of middling or more than middling fortune. Such, for example, are the duties on foreign wines and on coffee, chocolate, tea, sugar, and the like.
