The duties on the cheaper luxuries of home produce, meant for home consumption, fall fairly evenly on people of all ranks, in proportion to their respective spending. The poor pay the duties on malt, hops, beer, and ale through their own consumption; the rich pay them through both their own consumption and that of their servants.

It must be noted that the whole consumption of the lower ranks of people—those below the middling rank—is, in every country, much greater, not only in quantity but in value, than that of the middling rank and those above it. The total spending of the lower ranks is far greater than that of the upper ranks. In the first place, almost the whole capital of every country is distributed each year among the lower ranks as the wages of productive labour. Secondly, a large part of the revenue arising from both the rent of land and the profits of stock is distributed each year among the same rank, as the wages and upkeep of menial servants and other unproductive labourers. Thirdly, some part of the profits of stock belongs to the same rank, as a return on the employment of their small capitals. The profits made each year by small shopkeepers, tradesmen, and retailers of all kinds are everywhere very considerable, and make up a very considerable share of the annual produce. Fourthly and lastly, some part even of the rent of land belongs to the same rank—a considerable part to those somewhat below the middling rank, and a small part even to the lowest rank, since common labourers sometimes own an acre or two of land. So although the spending of these lower ranks, taken individually, is very small, the whole mass of it, taken together, always amounts to by far the largest portion of the whole spending of society; what remains of the annual produce of the country's land and labour, for the consumption of the upper ranks, is always much less, not only in quantity but in value. Taxes on spending that fall chiefly on the upper ranks, on the smaller portion of the annual produce, are therefore likely to be much less productive than either those that fall evenly on the spending of all ranks, or those that fall chiefly on the spending of the lower ranks—less productive than either those that fall evenly on the whole annual produce, or those that fall chiefly on the larger portion of it. The excise on the raw materials and manufacture of home-made fermented and spirituous liquors is accordingly, of all the various taxes on spending, by far the most productive; and this branch of the excise falls very much, perhaps chiefly, on the spending of the common people. In the year that ended on 5 July 1775, the gross produce of this branch of the excise came to £3,341,837 9s 9d.

It must always be remembered, however, that it is the luxuries, and not the necessary spending, of the lower ranks of people that should ever be taxed. The final payment of any tax on their necessary spending would fall entirely on the upper ranks—on the smaller portion of the annual produce, not the greater. Such a tax must in all cases either raise the wages of labour or reduce the demand for it. It could not raise wages without throwing the final payment of the tax onto the upper ranks. It could not reduce the demand for labour without reducing the annual produce of the country's land and labour, the fund out of which all taxes must finally be paid. Whatever state a tax of this kind reduced the demand for labour to, it would always raise wages higher than they would otherwise be in that state; and the final payment of this rise in wages must in all cases fall on the upper ranks of people.

Fermented liquors brewed, and spirituous liquors distilled, not for sale but for private use, are not in Great Britain liable to any excise duties. This exemption, meant to spare private families the hateful visits and examinations of the tax-collector, often makes the burden of those duties fall much more lightly on the rich than on the poor. It is true that distilling for private use is not very common, though it is done sometimes. But in the country, many middling and almost all rich and great families brew their own beer. Their strong beer therefore costs them eight shillings a barrel less than it costs the common brewer, who must add his profit on the tax as well as on all his other expenses. Such families therefore drink their beer at least nine or ten shillings a barrel cheaper than the common people can drink any liquor of the same quality—people who find it more convenient everywhere to buy their beer in small amounts from the brewery or the alehouse. In the same way, malt made for a private family's own use is not liable to the tax-collector's visit or examination; but in this case the family must pay a fixed composition of seven shillings and sixpence a head for the tax. Seven shillings and sixpence equal the excise on ten bushels of malt, a quantity fully equal to what all the members of any sober family—men, women, and children—are, on average, likely to consume. But in rich and great families, where country hospitality is much practised, the malt liquor consumed by the family members makes up only a small part of the household's consumption. Either because of this composition, however, or for other reasons, malting for private use is far less common than brewing for private use. It is hard to imagine any fair reason why those who brew or distil for private use should not be subject to a composition of the same kind.

It has often been said that a much lighter tax on malt could raise more revenue than is now drawn from all the heavy taxes on malt, beer, and ale—the chances of defrauding the revenue being far greater in a brewery than in a malt-house, and those who brew for private use being exempt from all duties or compositions, which is not the case with those who malt for private use.

In the porter breweries of London, a quarter of malt is commonly brewed into more than two and a half barrels—sometimes three barrels—of porter. The various taxes on malt come to six shillings a quarter, and those on strong ale and beer to eight shillings a barrel. In the porter brewery, then, the various taxes on malt, beer, and ale come to between twenty-six and thirty shillings on the produce of a quarter of malt. In country breweries for ordinary local sale, a quarter of malt is seldom brewed into less than two barrels of strong beer and one barrel of small beer, and often into two and a half barrels of strong beer. The various taxes on small beer come to one shilling and fourpence a barrel. In the country brewery, then, the various taxes on malt, beer, and ale seldom come to less than twenty-three shillings and fourpence, and often to twenty-six shillings, on the produce of a quarter of malt. Taking the whole kingdom on average, therefore, the total duties on malt, beer, and ale cannot be reckoned at less than twenty-four or twenty-five shillings on the produce of a quarter of malt. But it is said that by removing all the various duties on beer and ale, and trebling the malt tax—raising it from six to eighteen shillings a quarter of malt—this single tax could raise more revenue than is now drawn from all those heavier taxes.

In 1772, the old malt tax produced £722,023 11s 11d, the additional £356,776 7s 9¾ d. In 1773, the old tax produced £561,627 3s 7½ d, the additional £278,650 15s 3¾ d. In 1774, the old tax produced £624,614 17s 5¾ d, the additional £310,745 2s 8½ d. In 1775, the old tax produced £657,357 0s 8¼ d, the additional £323,785 12s 6¼ d. The four-year total is £3,835,580 12s 0¾ d, divided by four for an average over these four years of £958,895 3s 0d.

In 1772, the country excise produced £1,243,120 5s 3d and the London brewery £408,260 7s 2¾ d. In 1773, the country excise produced £1,245,808 3s 3d and the London brewery £405,406 17s 10½ d. In 1774, the country excise produced £1,246,373 14s 5½ d and the London brewery £320,601 18s 0¼ d. In 1775, the country excise produced £1,214,583 6s 1¼ d and the London brewery £463,670 7s 0¼ d. The four-year total is £6,547,832 19s 2¼ d, divided by four for an average over these four years of £1,636,958 4s 9½ d; to which, adding the average malt tax of £958,895 3s 0¼ d:
the whole of these various taxes comes to £2,595,835 7s 10d.
But by trebling the malt tax—raising it from six to eighteen shillings a quarter of malt—that single tax would produce £2,876,685 9s 0d, a sum that exceeds the foregoing by £280,832 1s 3d.

The old malt tax does, it is true, include a tax of four shillings on the hogshead of cider and another of ten shillings on the barrel of mum. In 1774, the tax on cider produced only £3,083 6s 8d. It probably fell somewhat short of its usual figure, since all the various taxes on cider produced less than normal that year. The tax on mum, though much heavier, is even less productive because that liquor is consumed less. But to set against whatever the ordinary yield of those two taxes may be, the so-called country excise includes, first, the old excise of six shillings and eightpence on the hogshead of cider; secondly, a like tax of six shillings and eightpence on the hogshead of verjuice; thirdly, another of eight shillings and ninepence on the hogshead of vinegar; and lastly, a fourth tax of elevenpence on the gallon of mead or metheglin. The produce of these various taxes will probably more than make up for that of the duties imposed by the so-called annual malt tax on cider and mum.

Malt is consumed not only in brewing beer and ale but in making low wines and spirits. If the malt tax were raised to eighteen shillings a quarter, it might be necessary to reduce some of the various excises imposed on those particular kinds of low wines and spirits that have malt among their materials. In what are called malt spirits, malt usually makes up only a third of the materials, the other two-thirds being either raw barley, or one-third barley and one-third wheat. In distilling malt spirits, both the opportunity and the temptation to smuggle are much greater than in a brewery or malt-house—the opportunity because the commodity is smaller in bulk and greater in value, and the temptation because of the higher duties, which came to 3s 10⅔ d on the gallon of spirits. (Though the duties laid directly on proof spirits come to only 2s 6d per gallon, these, added to the duties on the low wines from which they are distilled, come to 3s 10⅔ d. Both low wines and proof spirits are now rated, to prevent fraud, according to what they gauge in the wash.)
By raising the duties on malt and reducing those on distilling, both the opportunity and the temptation to smuggle would be lessened, which might bring about a still further increase in revenue.

For some time it has been the policy of Great Britain to discourage the consumption of spirituous liquors, because of their supposed tendency to ruin the health and corrupt the morals of the common people. Under this policy, the reduction of the duties on distilling should not be so great as to lower in any way the price of those liquors. Spirituous liquors might stay as dear as ever, while at the same time the wholesome and invigorating liquors of beer and ale could be considerably reduced in price. The people might thus be partly relieved of one of the burdens they now complain of most, while at the same time the revenue might be considerably increased.

Dr Davenant's objections to this change in the present system of excise duties seem to be without foundation. His objections are these: that the tax, instead of dividing itself fairly evenly—as it now does—among the profit of the maltster, that of the brewer, and that of the retailer, would, so far as it affected profit, fall entirely on the maltster; that the maltster could not so easily recover the amount of the tax through the raised price of his malt as the brewer and retailer can through the raised price of their liquor; and that so heavy a tax on malt might lower the rent and profit of barley land.

No tax can ever lower, for any considerable time, the rate of profit in any particular trade, which must always stay level with that of other trades nearby. The present duties on malt, beer, and ale do not affect the profits of the dealers in those commodities, who all recover the tax with an additional profit through the raised price of their goods. A tax may indeed make the goods it is laid on so dear as to reduce their consumption. But malt is consumed in malt liquors, and a tax of eighteen shillings a quarter of malt could hardly make those liquors dearer than the various taxes, coming to twenty-four or twenty-five shillings, do at present. On the contrary, those liquors would probably become cheaper, and their consumption would be more likely to increase than to fall.

It is not easy to see why it should be harder for the maltster to recover eighteen shillings through the raised price of his malt than it now is for the brewer to recover twenty-four or twenty-five, sometimes thirty, shillings through that of his liquor. The maltster, it is true, instead of a tax of six shillings, would have to advance one of eighteen shillings on every quarter of malt. But the brewer is at present obliged to advance a tax of twenty-four or twenty-five, sometimes thirty, shillings on every quarter of malt he brews. It could be no more inconvenient for the maltster to advance a lighter tax than it now is for the brewer to advance a heavier one. The maltster does not always keep in his granaries a stock of malt that will take longer to dispose of than the stock of beer and ale the brewer often keeps in his cellars. The maltster, therefore, may often get his money back as soon as the brewer. But whatever inconvenience the maltster might face from having to advance a heavier tax could easily be remedied by allowing him a few months' longer credit than the brewer is now commonly given.

Nothing could lower the rent and profit of barley land that did not lower the demand for barley. But a change of system that reduced the duties on a quarter of malt brewed into beer and ale from twenty-four or twenty-five shillings to eighteen would be more likely to increase that demand than to reduce it. The rent and profit of barley land, besides, must always be nearly equal to those of other equally fertile and equally well cultivated land. If they were less, some of the barley land would soon be turned to another use; and if they were greater, more land would soon be turned to growing barley. When the ordinary price of any particular produce of land is what may be called a monopoly price, a tax on it necessarily lowers the rent and profit of the land that grows it. A tax on the produce of those precious vineyards whose wine falls so far short of effective demand that its price is always above the natural proportion to that of other equally fertile and equally well cultivated land would necessarily lower the rent and profit of those vineyards. Since the price of the wines is already the highest that could be got for the quantity normally sent to market, it could not be raised higher without reducing that quantity; and the quantity could not be reduced without still greater loss, because the land could not be turned to any other equally valuable produce. The whole weight of the tax, therefore, would fall on the rent and profit—properly on the rent of the vineyard. When a new tax on sugar has been proposed, our sugar planters have often complained that the whole weight of such taxes fell not on the consumer but on the producer, since they had never been able to raise the price of their sugar after the tax above what it was before. The price had, it seems, been a monopoly price before the tax; and the arguments brought forward to show that sugar was an unfit subject of taxation perhaps proved that it was a fit one—the gains of monopolists, whenever they can be reached, being certainly of all subjects the most fit to tax. But the ordinary price of barley has never been a monopoly price, and the rent and profit of barley land have never been above their natural proportion to those of other equally fertile and equally well cultivated land. The various taxes laid on malt, beer, and ale have never lowered the price of barley, and have never reduced the rent and profit of barley land. The price of malt to the brewer has constantly risen in proportion to the taxes laid on it; and those taxes, together with the various duties on beer and ale, have constantly either raised the price or—what comes to the same thing—lowered the quality of those commodities to the consumer. The final payment of those taxes has constantly fallen on the consumer, not the producer.

The only people likely to suffer from the change of system proposed here are those who brew for their own private use. But the exemption these superior people now enjoy from the very heavy taxes paid by the poor labourer and artisan is surely most unjust and unequal, and ought to be removed even if this change were never to take place. It has probably been the interest of this superior order of people, however, that has so far prevented a change of system which could hardly fail both to increase the revenue and to relieve the people.

Besides duties such as the customs and excise mentioned above, there are several others that affect the price of goods more unequally and more indirectly. Of this kind are the duties called peages in French, which in old Saxon times were called duties of passage, and which seem to have been originally set up for the same purpose as our turnpike tolls, or the tolls on our canals and navigable rivers—the upkeep of the road or the waterway. When applied to such purposes, those duties are most properly charged according to the bulk or weight of the goods. Since they were originally local and provincial duties for local and provincial purposes, their administration was in most cases entrusted to the particular town, parish, or lordship where they were collected, those communities being supposed in some way to be accountable for how the money was applied. The sovereign, who is entirely unaccountable, has in many countries taken the administration of those duties to himself; and although in most cases he has greatly increased the duty, in many he has entirely neglected its application. If the turnpike tolls of Great Britain should ever become one of the government's resources, the example of many other nations shows what the consequence would probably be. Such tolls are no doubt finally paid by the consumer; but the consumer is not taxed in proportion to his spending when he pays not according to the value but according to the bulk or weight of what he consumes. When such duties are imposed not according to bulk or weight but according to the supposed value of the goods, they become in effect a kind of inland customs or excise, which greatly obstructs the most important of all branches of commerce—the internal commerce of the country.

In some small states, duties similar to those passage duties are imposed on goods carried across the territory, by land or water, from one foreign country to another. In some countries these are called transit duties. Some of the little Italian states situated on the Po and the rivers that flow into it draw some revenue from duties of this kind, which are paid entirely by foreigners, and which are perhaps the only duties one state can impose on the subjects of another without obstructing in any way its own industry or commerce. The most important transit duty in the world is the one levied by the King of Denmark on all merchant ships that pass through the Sound.

Such taxes on luxuries—as most of the customs and excise duties are—although they all fall indifferently on every kind of income, and are finally paid, with no compensation, by whoever consumes the commodities they are laid on, nevertheless do not always fall equally or proportionally on the income of every individual. Since each man's taste governs how much he consumes, each man contributes according to his taste rather than in proportion to his income: the extravagant contribute more, and the thrifty less, than their proper share. While a man of great fortune is still a minor, he commonly contributes very little, through his consumption, towards supporting the state from whose protection he draws a great income. Those who live in another country contribute nothing through their consumption towards supporting the government of the country where the source of their income lies. If in that latter country there is no land tax, nor any considerable duty on the transfer of either movable or immovable property—as is the case in Ireland—such absentees may draw a great income from the protection of a government to whose support they do not contribute a single shilling. This inequality is likely to be greatest in a country whose government is in some respects subordinate to and dependent on that of some other. The people who hold the most extensive property in the dependent country will, in that case, generally choose to live in the governing country. Ireland is in exactly this situation, and so we cannot wonder that the proposal of a tax on absentees should be so very popular there. It might perhaps be a little hard to determine what sort, or what degree, of absence would make a man liable to be taxed as an absentee, or at what precise time the tax should begin or end. But apart from this very peculiar situation, any inequality in individuals' contributions that may arise from such taxes is much more than offset by the very thing that causes the inequality—namely, that every man's contribution is entirely voluntary, since it is entirely in his power either to consume or not to consume the taxed commodity. Where such taxes are properly assessed, and on proper commodities, they are therefore paid with less grumbling than any other. When they are advanced by the merchant or manufacturer, the consumer who finally pays them soon comes to confuse them with the price of the commodities, and almost forgets that he is paying any tax at all. Such taxes are, or can be, perfectly certain; they can be assessed so as to leave no doubt about either what is to be paid or when it is to be paid—about either the amount or the time of payment. Whatever uncertainty there may sometimes be, either in the customs duties of Great Britain or in similar duties in other countries, it cannot arise from the nature of those duties, but from the inaccurate or unskilful way in which the law that imposes them is worded.

Taxes on luxuries generally are, and always may be, paid bit by bit, as the contributors happen to need to buy the goods they are laid on. In their timing and method of payment, they are, or can be, the most convenient of all taxes. On the whole, then, such taxes are perhaps as much in keeping with the first three of the four general maxims of taxation as any other. They offend in every respect against the fourth.

In proportion to what they bring into the public treasury of the state, such taxes always take, or keep, out of the people's pockets more than almost any other taxes. They seem to do this in all four of the ways in which it is possible to do it.

First, the collection of such taxes, even when imposed in the most judicious way, requires a great number of customs and excise officers, whose salaries and perquisites are a real tax on the people that brings nothing into the treasury of the state. This expense, it must be granted, is more moderate in Great Britain than in most other countries. In the year that ended on 5 July 1775, the gross produce of the various duties under the management of the commissioners of excise in England came to £5,507,308 18s 8¼ d, collected at a cost of little more than five and a half per cent. From this gross produce, however, must be deducted what was paid out in bounties and drawbacks on the export of excisable goods, which brings the net produce below five million. (The net produce of that year, after deducting all expenses and allowances, came to £4,975,652 19s 6d.) The collection of the salt duty—also an excise duty, but under a different management—is much more expensive. The net customs revenue does not reach two and a half million, and is collected at a cost of more than ten per cent in officers' salaries and other incidentals. But the perquisites of customs officers are everywhere much greater than their salaries—at some ports more than double or triple them. So if salaries and other incidentals come to more than ten per cent of the net customs revenue, the whole cost of collecting that revenue, in salaries and perquisites together, may come to more than twenty or thirty per cent. Excise officers receive few or no perquisites; and the administration of that branch of the revenue, being more recently established, is in general less corrupted than that of the customs, into which the passage of time has introduced and sanctioned many abuses. By charging on malt the whole revenue now collected by the various duties on malt and malt liquors, a saving of more than £50,000, it is supposed, could be made in the annual cost of the excise. By confining the customs duties to a few kinds of goods, and collecting them under the excise laws, a much greater saving could probably be made in the annual cost of the customs.

Secondly, such taxes necessarily obstruct or discourage certain branches of industry. Since they always raise the price of the taxed commodity, they discourage its consumption that far, and consequently its production. If it is a home-grown or home-manufactured commodity, less labour is employed in raising and producing it. If it is a foreign commodity whose price the tax raises in this way, commodities of the same kind made at home may indeed gain some advantage in the home market, and a greater quantity of domestic industry may be turned towards making them. But although this rise in the price of a foreign commodity may encourage domestic industry in one particular branch, it necessarily discourages it in almost every other. The dearer the Birmingham manufacturer buys his foreign wine, the cheaper he necessarily sells the part of his hardware with which—or, what comes to the same thing, with the price of which—he buys it. That part of his hardware therefore becomes worth less to him, and he has less encouragement to work at it. The dearer consumers in one country pay for the surplus produce of another, the cheaper they necessarily sell the part of their own surplus produce with which—or, what comes to the same thing, with the price of which—they buy it. That part of their own surplus produce becomes worth less to them, and they have less encouragement to increase its quantity. All taxes on consumable commodities, therefore, tend to reduce the quantity of productive labour below what it would otherwise be—either in making the taxed commodities, if they are home commodities, or in making the goods with which those are bought, if they are foreign. Such taxes, too, always alter, more or less, the natural direction of national industry, and turn it into a channel always different from, and generally less advantageous than, the one it would have followed of its own accord.

Thirdly, the hope of evading such taxes by smuggling frequently gives rise to forfeitures and other penalties that utterly ruin the smuggler—a man who, though no doubt highly blameable for breaking the laws of his country, is often incapable of breaking the laws of natural justice, and would have been in every way an excellent citizen had not his country's laws made a crime of what nature never meant to be one. In those corrupt governments where there is at least a general suspicion of much needless expense and great misuse of the public revenue, the laws that guard it are little respected. Not many people are scrupulous about smuggling when, without perjury, they can find an easy and safe chance to do it. To pretend to have any scruple about buying smuggled goods—though doing so plainly encourages the breaking of the revenue laws and the perjury that almost always goes with it—would, in most countries, be regarded as one of those pedantic bits of hypocrisy which, far from gaining anyone's respect, only expose the person who affects to practise them to the suspicion of being a greater rogue than most of his neighbours. By this indulgence of the public, the smuggler is often encouraged to keep up a trade which he is thereby taught to think of as in some measure innocent; and when the full severity of the revenue laws is about to fall on him, he is often inclined to defend with violence what he has grown used to regarding as his rightful property. From being at first perhaps imprudent rather than criminal, he too often becomes in the end one of the boldest and most determined breakers of the laws of society. With the ruin of the smuggler, his capital, which had before been employed in maintaining productive labour, is absorbed either into the revenue of the state or into that of the revenue officer, and is employed in maintaining unproductive labour, to the diminution of the general capital of society and of the useful industry it might otherwise have maintained.

Fourthly, such taxes, by subjecting at least the dealers in the taxed commodities to the frequent visits and hateful examinations of the tax-collectors, sometimes expose them to some degree of oppression, and always to much trouble and aggravation; and although aggravation, as has already been said, is not strictly speaking an expense, it is certainly equivalent to the expense at which any man would be willing to buy himself free of it. The excise laws, though more effective for the purpose they were set up for, are in this respect more vexatious than the customs laws. When a merchant has imported goods subject to certain customs duties, has paid those duties, and has lodged the goods in his warehouse, he is in most cases not liable to any further trouble or aggravation from the customs officer. It is otherwise with goods subject to excise duties. The dealers get no respite from the continual visits and examinations of the excise officers. The excise duties are for this reason more unpopular than the customs duties, and so are the officers who collect them. It is claimed of those officers that, although in general they perhaps do their duty fully as well as those of the customs, yet, since that duty obliges them to be frequently very troublesome to some of their neighbours, they commonly take on a certain hardness of character that the others often do not. This remark, however, may very likely be merely the suggestion of fraudulent dealers whose smuggling is either prevented or detected by the officers' diligence.

The inconveniences that are perhaps to some degree inseparable from taxes on consumable commodities fall as lightly on the people of Great Britain as on those of any other country whose government is nearly as expensive. Our state is not perfect, and could be improved; but it is as good as, or better than, that of most of our neighbours.

Because of the notion that duties on consumable goods were taxes on merchants' profits, those duties have in some countries been charged again at every successive sale of the goods. If the profits of the importing merchant or the manufacturing merchant were taxed, fairness seemed to require that the profits of all the middle buyers who came between either of them and the consumer should likewise be taxed. The famous alcavala of Spain seems to have been set up on this principle. It was at first a tax of ten per cent, afterwards of fourteen per cent, and is at present only six per cent on the sale of every kind of property, movable or immovable; and it is charged again every time the property is sold. (Mémoires concernant les Droits, etc., vol. i, p. 15.) The collection of this tax requires a multitude of revenue officers, enough to watch the movement of goods not only from one province to another but from one shop to another. It subjects not only the dealers in some kinds of goods, but those in all kinds—every farmer, every manufacturer, every merchant and shopkeeper—to the continual visits and examinations of the tax-collectors. Through most of a country where a tax of this kind exists, nothing can be produced for distant sale. The produce of every part of the country must be matched to the consumption of its own neighbourhood. It is to the alcavala, accordingly, that Ustariz attributes the ruin of the manufactures of Spain. He might also have attributed to it the decline of agriculture, since it is laid not only on manufactures but on the raw produce of the land.

In the kingdom of Naples there is a similar tax of three per cent on the value of all contracts, and consequently on that of all contracts of sale. It is both lighter than the Spanish tax, and most towns and parishes are allowed to pay a composition in place of it. They collect this composition however they please, generally in a way that does not interrupt the internal commerce of the place. The Neapolitan tax, therefore, is nowhere near as ruinous as the Spanish one.

The uniform system of taxation that, with a few exceptions of no great importance, applies in all the different parts of the united kingdom of Great Britain leaves the internal commerce of the country—the inland and coasting trade—almost entirely free. The inland trade is almost perfectly free; and most goods can be carried from one end of the kingdom to the other without any permit or pass, and without being subject to questioning, visits, or examination by the revenue officers. There are a few exceptions, but they are such as can give no interruption to any important branch of the country's inland commerce. Goods carried coastwise do, it is true, require certificates or coast-cockets. But apart from coals, almost all the rest are duty-free. This freedom of internal commerce, the effect of the uniformity of the system of taxation, is perhaps one of the chief causes of the prosperity of Great Britain—every great country being necessarily the best and most extensive market for most of the products of its own industry. If the same freedom, through the same uniformity, could be extended to Ireland and the plantations, both the grandeur of the state and the prosperity of every part of the empire would probably be still greater than at present.

In France, the different revenue laws that apply in the different provinces require a multitude of revenue officers to surround not only the kingdom's frontiers but those of almost every individual province, in order either to prevent the import of certain goods or to subject it to certain duties—to the no small interruption of the country's internal commerce. Some provinces are allowed to compound for the gabelle, or salt tax; others are exempted from it altogether. Some provinces are exempt from the exclusive sale of tobacco that the farmers-general enjoy through most of the kingdom. The aides, which correspond to the excise in England, vary greatly from province to province. Some provinces are exempt from them and pay a composition or equivalent instead. In those where they apply and are farmed out, there are many local duties that do not extend beyond a particular town or district. The traites, which correspond to our customs, divide the kingdom into three great parts: first, the provinces subject to the tariff of 1664, called the provinces of the five great farms, which include Picardy, Normandy, and most of the interior provinces of the kingdom; secondly, the provinces subject to the tariff of 1667, called the provinces reckoned foreign, which include most of the frontier provinces; and thirdly, those provinces said to be treated as foreign, which—because they are allowed free commerce with foreign countries—are, in their trade with the other provinces of France, subject to the same duties as other foreign countries. These are Alsace; the three bishoprics of Metz, Toul, and Verdun; and the three cities of Dunkirk, Bayonne, and Marseilles. Both in the provinces of the five great farms (so called from an ancient division of the customs duties into five great branches, each originally the subject of a separate farm, though they are now all united into one) and in those reckoned foreign, there are many local duties that do not extend beyond a particular town or district. There are some such even in the provinces treated as foreign, particularly in the city of Marseilles. There is no need to point out how greatly both the restraints on the country's internal commerce, and the number of revenue officers, must be multiplied in order to guard the frontiers of all these different provinces and districts subject to such different systems of taxation.

Over and above the general restraints arising from this complicated system of revenue laws, the wine trade (after corn, perhaps the most important product of France) is, in most of the provinces, subject to particular restraints arising from the favour shown to the vineyards of some provinces and districts over others. The provinces most famous for their wines, I believe, will be found to be those where the trade in that article is subject to the fewest restraints of this kind. The extensive market such provinces enjoy encourages good management both in cultivating their vineyards and in the subsequent preparation of their wines.

Such varied and complicated revenue laws are not peculiar to France. The little duchy of Milan is divided into six provinces, in each of which there is a different system of taxation with regard to several different kinds of consumable goods. The still smaller territories of the Duke of Parma are divided into three or four, each with a system of its own in the same way. Under such absurd management, nothing but the great fertility of the soil and the kindness of the climate could keep such countries from soon relapsing into the lowest state of poverty and barbarism.

Taxes on consumable commodities may be collected either by an administration whose officers are appointed by the government and are directly accountable to it—in which case the revenue must vary from year to year with the occasional variations in the produce of the tax—or they may be let in farm for a fixed rent, the farmer being allowed to appoint his own officers, who, though obliged to collect the tax in the manner the law directs, are under his immediate supervision and directly accountable to him. The best and most economical way of collecting a tax can never be by farming it out. Over and above what is needed to pay the agreed rent, the officers' salaries, and the whole cost of administration, the farmer must always draw from the produce of the tax a certain profit, proportioned at least to the money he advances, the risk he runs, the trouble he takes, and the knowledge and skill required to manage so complicated a business. By setting up an administration under their own immediate supervision, of the same kind the farmer establishes, the government could at least save this profit, which is almost always extortionate. To farm any considerable branch of the public revenue requires either a great capital or great credit, circumstances that would by themselves restrict competition for such an undertaking to a very small number of people. Of the few who have this capital or credit, a still smaller number have the necessary knowledge or experience—another circumstance that restricts competition still further. The very few who are in a position to compete find it more in their interest to combine, becoming partners instead of competitors, and, when the farm is put up to auction, to offer no rent but what is far below its real value. In countries where the public revenues are farmed out, the farmers are generally the most opulent people. Their wealth alone would excite the public's indignation; and the vanity that almost always goes with such upstart fortunes, the foolish ostentation with which they commonly display that wealth, excite that indignation still more.

The farmers of the public revenue never find the laws too severe that punish any attempt to evade payment of a tax. They have no compassion for the contributors, who are not their subjects, and whose universal bankruptcy, were it to happen the day after the farm expired, would barely affect their interest. In the greatest emergencies of the state, when the sovereign's anxiety for the exact payment of his revenue is necessarily greatest, they seldom fail to complain that, without laws more rigorous than those then in force, they will be unable to pay even the usual rent. In those moments of public distress, their demands cannot be disputed. The revenue laws therefore grow gradually more and more severe. The most bloodthirsty are always to be found in countries where most of the public revenue is farmed out; the mildest, in countries where it is collected under the sovereign's own immediate supervision. Even a bad sovereign feels more compassion for his people than can ever be expected from the farmers of his revenue. He knows that the lasting grandeur of his family depends on the prosperity of his people, and he will never knowingly ruin that prosperity for the sake of any momentary interest of his own. It is otherwise with the farmers of his revenue, whose grandeur may often be the result of the ruin, not the prosperity, of his people.

Sometimes a tax is not only farmed for a certain rent, but the farmer also has the monopoly of the taxed commodity. In France, the duties on tobacco and salt are collected in this way. In such cases the farmer levies on the people not one but two extortionate profits—the farmer's profit and the still more extortionate one of the monopolist. Tobacco being a luxury, every man is free to buy it or not as he chooses; but salt being a necessity, every man is obliged to buy a certain quantity of it from the farmer, because if he did not, it is presumed he would buy it from some smuggler. The taxes on both commodities are extortionate. The temptation to smuggle is consequently irresistible to many people, while at the same time the harshness of the law and the vigilance of the farmer's officers make yielding to the temptation almost certainly ruinous. The smuggling of salt and tobacco sends several hundred people to the galleys every year, besides a very considerable number it sends to the gallows. Those taxes, collected in this way, yield a very considerable revenue to the government. In 1767, the farm of tobacco was let for twenty-two million five hundred and forty-one thousand two hundred and seventy-eight livres a year, and that of salt for thirty-six million four hundred and ninety-two thousand four hundred and four livres. In both cases the farm was to begin in 1768 and last six years. Those who count the blood of the people as nothing compared with the revenue of the prince may perhaps approve of this method of collecting taxes. Similar taxes and monopolies of salt and tobacco have been set up in many other countries, particularly in the Austrian and Prussian dominions and in most of the states of Italy.

In France, most of the actual revenue of the crown comes from eight different sources: the taille, the capitation, the two vingtièmes, the gabelles, the aides, the traites, the domaine, and the farm of tobacco. The last five are, in most of the provinces, farmed out. The first three are everywhere collected by an administration under the immediate supervision and direction of the government; and it is universally acknowledged that, in proportion to what they take out of the people's pockets, they bring more into the prince's treasury than the other five, whose administration is much more wasteful and expensive.

The finances of France seem, in their present state, to allow of three very obvious reforms. First, by abolishing the taille and the capitation, and increasing the number of vingtièmes so as to produce an extra revenue equal to the amount of those other taxes, the revenue of the crown could be preserved; the cost of collection could be much reduced; the aggravation of the lower ranks of people that the taille and capitation cause could be entirely prevented; and the upper ranks need be no more burdened than most of them are at present. The vingtième, as I have already noted, is a tax very nearly of the same kind as what is called the land tax of England. The burden of the taille, it is acknowledged, falls finally on the proprietors of land; and since most of the capitation is assessed on those subject to the taille, at so much per pound of that other tax, the final payment of most of it must likewise fall on the same order of people. So although the number of vingtièmes were increased to produce an extra revenue equal to the amount of both those taxes, the upper ranks need be no more burdened than they are at present—though many individuals would, no doubt, because of the great inequalities with which the taille is commonly assessed on the estates and tenants of different individuals. The interest and opposition of such favoured subjects are the obstacles most likely to prevent this, or any other reform of the same kind. Secondly, by making the gabelle, the aides, the traites, the taxes on tobacco, and all the various customs and excises uniform in all parts of the kingdom, those taxes could be collected at much less expense, and the internal commerce of the kingdom could be made as free as that of England. Thirdly and lastly, by placing all those taxes under an administration directly supervised and directed by the government, the extortionate profits of the farmers-general could be added to the revenue of the state. The opposition arising from the private interest of individuals is likely to be as effective in preventing the last two reforms as the first.

The French system of taxation seems in every respect inferior to the British. In Great Britain, ten million pounds sterling are collected each year from fewer than eight million people, without its being possible to say that any particular order is oppressed. From the Collections of the Abbé Expilly, and from the observations of the author of the Essay upon the Legislation and Commerce of Corn, it appears probable that France, including the provinces of Lorraine and Bar, contains about twenty-three or twenty-four million people—three times the number, perhaps, of Great Britain. The soil and climate of France are better than those of Great Britain. The country has been much longer in a state of improvement and cultivation, and is on that account better stocked with all those things that take a long time to raise and accumulate—great towns, and convenient, well-built houses, both in town and country. With these advantages, one might expect that in France a revenue of thirty million could be collected for the support of the state with as little inconvenience as a revenue of ten million is in Great Britain. In 1765 and 1766, the whole revenue paid into the treasury of France, according to the best though, I admit, very imperfect accounts I could get of it, usually ran between 308 and 325 million livres—that is, it did not amount to fifteen million sterling, not half of what might have been expected had the people contributed in the same proportion to their numbers as the people of Great Britain. Yet the people of France, it is generally acknowledged, are much more oppressed by taxes than the people of Great Britain. France, however, is certainly the great empire in Europe which, after Great Britain, enjoys the mildest and most indulgent government.

In Holland, the heavy taxes on the necessaries of life have, it is said, ruined their principal manufactures, and are likely gradually to discourage even their fisheries and their shipbuilding trade. The taxes on the necessaries of life are slight in Great Britain, and no manufacture has so far been ruined by them. The British taxes that bear hardest on manufactures are some duties on the import of raw materials, particularly raw silk. The revenue of the States-General and of the various cities, however, is said to come to more than five million two hundred and fifty thousand pounds sterling; and since the inhabitants of the United Provinces can hardly be supposed to number more than a third of those of Great Britain, they must, in proportion to their numbers, be much more heavily taxed.

After all the proper subjects of taxation have been used up, if the needs of the state still call for new taxes, they must be laid on improper ones. The taxes on the necessaries of life, therefore, may be no reflection on the wisdom of that republic which, in order to win and keep its independence, has—despite its great frugality—been drawn into such expensive wars that it has had to contract great debts. The peculiar countries of Holland and Zealand, besides, require a considerable expense merely to preserve their existence, or to keep from being swallowed up by the sea, which must have helped to increase considerably the load of taxes in those two provinces. The republican form of government seems to be the chief support of the present grandeur of Holland. The owners of great capitals, the great mercantile families, generally have either some direct share in, or some indirect influence over, the administration of that government. For the sake of the respect and authority they derive from this position, they are willing to live in a country where their capital, if they employ it themselves, will bring them less profit, and if they lend it to another, less interest; and where the very moderate income they can draw from it will buy less of the necessaries and comforts of life than in any other part of Europe. The residence of such wealthy people necessarily keeps alive, despite all these disadvantages, a certain degree of industry in the country. Any public calamity that destroyed the republican form of government, that threw the whole administration into the hands of nobles and soldiers, that wiped out altogether the importance of those wealthy merchants, would soon make it disagreeable to them to live in a country where they were no longer likely to be much respected. They would move both their residence and their capital to some other country, and the industry and commerce of Holland would soon follow the capitals that supported them.
